title: Cup with Handle
teaches: The cup with handle as we trade it: a leader that ran at least 30% rests in a smooth rounded U for seven weeks or more, climbs back near the old high, then dips into a quiet handle of five sessions or more that sits above the cup's midpoint, drifts down and holds the 50-day; the buy is the trade through the handle high at market in regular hours, the stop a few cents under the day's low and never past the handle low, a third off at 3R and 5R with the rest on the trail, and a loss taken at the stop is the plan working.

facts.quote: Cup-with-handle patterns are shaped like the silhouette of a tea cup viewed from the side.
facts.claim: IBD: a cup with handle is shaped like a tea cup seen from the side.

facts.quote: Cups should show smooth action on the left and right sides of the pattern.
facts.claim: IBD: both sides of a cup should be smooth.

facts.quote: There shouldn't be jagged edges or many wild weekly swings of 10% to 15% or more.
facts.claim: IBD: no jagged edges or many wild weekly swings of 10% to 15% or more.

facts.quote: V-shaped patterns are less reliable.
facts.claim: IBD: V-shaped patterns are less reliable.

facts.quote: The pattern's basic requirements start with a run up of at least 30% before the stock turns down into a consolidation.
facts.claim: IBD: the cup needs a run up of at least 30% before it.

facts.quote: A proper cup base needs to span a minimum of seven weeks, while a flat base can be as short as five weeks.
facts.claim: IBD: a cup spans at least seven weeks.

facts.quote: The base must be at least seven weeks long, including the handle.
facts.claim: IBD: at least seven weeks, the handle included.

facts.quote: They range from seven weeks to as long as 65 weeks in length, with many forming over three to six months.
facts.claim: IBD: cups run 7 to 65 weeks, many forming over three to six months.

facts.quote: The size of the decline, or correction, in a cup base should generally be between 12% and 33%.
facts.claim: IBD: a cup's decline is generally between 12% and 33%.

facts.quote: In bear markets, cups can run as deep as 50%.
facts.claim: IBD: in bear markets cups can run as deep as 50%.

facts.quote: to correct 1-1/2 to 2-1/2 times the market averages
facts.claim: IBD: a growth stock's cup corrects 1.5 to 2.5 times the market averages.

facts.quote: A proper handle forms in the upper half of a base and drifts slightly downward along its price lows.
facts.claim: IBD: a proper handle forms in the upper half and drifts slightly down along its lows.

facts.quote: In the handle, the midpoint of the handle's high and low marks should be above the midpoint of the high and low of the left side of the cup
facts.claim: IBD: the handle's midpoint sits above the cup's midpoint.

facts.quote: Handles that form too low present added risk of failure during breakouts.
facts.claim: IBD: handles that form too low fail more often.

facts.quote: Second, a handle should generally form above the 50-day or 10-week moving averages.
facts.claim: IBD: a handle generally forms above the 50-day line.

facts.quote: Handles must be at least five days long, and typically last for several weeks.
facts.claim: IBD: handles are at least five days long.

facts.quote: If it's shorter than five days, it's not a handle.
facts.claim: IBD: under five days it is not a handle.

facts.quote: Stocks with wedging handles have a higher failure rate and often are seen in late-stage bases
facts.claim: IBD: wedging handles fail more often and show up in late-stage bases.

facts.quote: Overeager handles that wedge upward tend to fail, while handles that drift lower foreshadow assertive action.
facts.claim: IBD: handles that wedge up tend to fail; handles that drift lower lead to strong moves.

facts.quote: A wedging handle with no shakeouts is a sign to steer clear.
facts.claim: IBD: a wedging handle with no shakeouts is a reason to stay away.

facts.quote: Volume should mostly ease until the breakout.
facts.claim: IBD: volume mostly eases until the breakout.

facts.quote: Volume should dry up, evidence that the weak holders are just about gone.
facts.claim: IBD: volume in the handle dries up as weak holders leave.

facts.quote: Handles should have areas of tight trading and days or weeks where volume contracts sharply.
facts.claim: IBD: handles show tight trading and sharp volume contraction.

facts.quote: The buy point is located by taking the highest price in the handle and adding 10 cents.
facts.claim: IBD's buy point is the handle's highest price plus 10 cents.

facts.quote: the rule says to sell all your shares of a stock if it falls 7% or 8% below the price at which you bought it.
facts.claim: IBD's general loss limit is 7% or 8% below the purchase price.

facts.quote: It's usually best to buy when a stock breaks out from a first-stage or second-stage base.
facts.claim: IBD: it is usually best to buy a first- or second-stage base.

facts.quote: Breakouts from late-stage bases will often blow up.
facts.claim: IBD: late-stage breakouts often blow up.

facts.quote: Once your stock has broken out, take most of your profits when they reach 20% to 25%.
facts.claim: IBD's general profit rule: take most profits at 20% to 25%.

facts.quote: The Cup & Handle is the corrective action after a powerful stock advance.
facts.claim: Zanger: the cup is the rest after a powerful advance.

facts.quote: The stock will sell off into the correction in a downward fashion for maybe 20 to 35 percent off the old high point.
facts.claim: Zanger: the cup falls maybe 20% to 35% off the old high.

facts.quote: The handle is generally about 5% below the old high point. A handle that is any lower is generally a defective stock and contains higher risk for failure.
facts.claim: Zanger: the handle sits about 5% below the old high; lower is riskier.

facts.quote: The time to buy the stock, is as it emerges into new highs at the top of the handle and not the old high point set some 8 to 12 weeks ago.
facts.claim: Zanger buys as it emerges into new highs at the top of the handle.

facts.quote: the best stocks with this formation are found at the beginning of a market move after a good market correction, and not during, or at the end of a major market advance.
facts.claim: Zanger: the best cups come at the start of a market move after a correction.

facts.quote: The cup should be U-shaped, not V-shaped, but allow variations.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: the cup is U-shaped, not V-shaped.

facts.quote: From 7 to 65 weeks (allow variations).
facts.claim: Bulkowski: a cup lasts 7 to 65 weeks.

facts.quote: 1 week minimum with no maximum, forming in the upper half of the cup.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: the handle lasts at least a week and forms in the upper half.

facts.quote: The handle low (point C) is a good place to put a stop. Raise the stop as price rises.
facts.claim: Bulkowski puts the stop at the handle low and raises it as price rises.

facts.quote: buy when price closes above the right cup rim
facts.claim: Bulkowski buys on a close above the right rim.

facts.quote: A V-shaped bottom would be considered too sharp of a reversal to qualify.
facts.claim: StockCharts: a V-shaped bottom is too sharp to qualify.

facts.quote: the handle should not extend into the lower half of the cup.
facts.claim: AAII: the handle should not reach into the lower half of the cup.

facts.quote: prices should have advanced at least 30% from the last intermediate low.
facts.claim: AAII: price should have advanced at least 30% from the last intermediate low.

facts.quote: Stop first (by default a few cents under the day's low or the prior day's low, F62); the size comes from the stop; if the honest stop does not fit the risk, skip the trade.
facts.claim: A3: stop first, a few cents under the day's low; the size comes from the stop; if the honest stop does not fit, skip.

facts.quote: The stop is the exit. It only moves up, never down or wider. The one exception is the gap rule (B20).
facts.claim: A4: the stop is the exit; it only moves up, never wider; the gap rule is the one exception.

facts.quote: Shares = account × risk % ÷ (entry − stop), rounded down, then capped: the size is the SMALLER of the risk-based size and the position cap
facts.claim: A5: shares are account times risk percent, divided by entry minus stop, rounded down, then capped.

facts.quote: "I almost never take a loss greater than 3%": the stop usually sits within about 3% of the buy (a loss on the position, not the account).
facts.claim: A13: the stop usually sits within about 3% of the buy.

facts.quote: Move the stop to breakeven at 2R to 5R, ideally. The first trim: the hard rule is a third at 3R; ideally anywhere from 3R to 6R, and in practice he mostly waits for 5R.
facts.claim: B19: breakeven between 2R and 5R; the hard rule for the first trim is a third at 3R.

facts.quote: A gap against the stop: the first 30 minutes of the gap-down day decide. The low of the first 30-minute bar is the new stop.
facts.claim: B20: on a gap through the stop, the first 30-minute low is the new stop.

facts.quote: With a ceiling: if the first 30 minutes take the loss past 2R, get out.
facts.claim: B20's ceiling: if the first 30 minutes take the loss past 2R, get out.

facts.quote: No new buys in the 3 days before an earnings report; hold through a report only if the trade is up 5R.
facts.claim: B22: no new buys in the 3 days before a report; hold through one only if up 5R.

facts.quote: No chasing: never buy more than 4% above the buy point.
facts.claim: C28: never buy more than 4% above the buy point.

facts.quote: Chasing costs size, not risk: the stop stays under the buy point, so the distance grows and the shares shrink (A5).
facts.claim: C28: chasing costs size, because the stop stays put and the distance grows.

facts.quote: Too stretched to buy: skip a long that is more than 10% above its 10-day average.
facts.claim: C29: skip a long more than 10% above its 10-day average.

facts.quote: After the first third at 3R: another third at 5R, then trail the last third; adjustable.
facts.claim: E51: another third at 5R, then trail the last third.

facts.quote: Default trail: the 10-day average for fast movers, the 21-day for steadier ones; sell on a close below it.
facts.claim: E52: trail the 10-day for fast movers, the 21-day for steadier ones; sell on a close below it.

facts.quote: Entries are market orders.
facts.claim: E57: entries are market orders.

facts.quote: No new buys outside regular trading hours.
facts.claim: E58: no new buys outside regular hours.

facts.quote: The stop sits a few cents under the day's low, not exactly on it.
facts.claim: F62: the stop sits a few cents under the day's low.

facts.quote: The market reading as a guide (A10): Green, full risk per grade and up to 10 positions; Yellow, smaller and fewer; Orange, only A+ setups; Red, mostly cash and shorts.
facts.claim: F65: Green full risk; Yellow smaller and fewer; Orange only A+; Red mostly cash and shorts.

facts.quote: After a market correction, when the reading turns Green again, start with a few positions and add more only as the first ones work
facts.claim: F68: after a correction, start with a few positions and add as they work.

facts.quote: After a stop-out, buy again only if the setup triggers again, as a new trade with its own stop and every rule.
facts.claim: B21: after a stop-out, buy again only on a new trigger, as a new trade.

facts.quote: Setup grades set the size: A and B setups at normal size; A+ sized up; B- or lower sized down.
facts.claim: D38: A and B normal size, A+ sized up, B- or lower sized down.

facts.quote: In a Red market: mostly cash, plus shorts below the 200-day.
facts.claim: D46: in a Red market, mostly cash plus shorts below the 200-day.

facts.quote: A climax run on your own long (Bracco's parabolic burst): sell a big part into it, a judgment call.
facts.claim: C34: sell a big part of a long into a climax run.

facts.quote: a 3-5 day final leg: three straight up days, two straight overnight gap ups, two of three days of range expansion, two days of rising volume, and a gap up on the climax day
facts.claim: B26: the parabolic burst is a 3 to 5 day final leg of up days, gaps, range expansion and rising volume.

facts.quote: Grading a setup (A+, A, B, B-) is discretionary and hard to define; no fixed checklist is taught as ours.
facts.claim: E50: grading is discretionary; no fixed checklist is ours.

facts.quote: The pivot is the highest price in the handle.
facts.claim: The pivot is the handle's highest price.

facts.quote: IBD adds 10 cents; with market orders the 10 cents does not matter.
facts.claim: IBD's 10 cents does not matter with a market order.

facts.quote: Price trades above the pivot during regular hours. Buy with a market order.
facts.claim: The trigger: price trades above the pivot in regular hours; buy at market.

facts.quote: The stock rose at least 30% from its lowest low of the prior 6 months (120 sessions) to the left-side high.
facts.claim: At least 30% from the lowest low of the prior 6 months to the left-side high.

facts.quote: At least 7 weeks (35 sessions) from the left-side high to the day before the breakout, the handle included.
facts.claim: At least 7 weeks, the handle included.

facts.quote: A rounded U, not a V: at least 30% of the cup's bars have their low in the cup's bottom quarter.
facts.claim: A rounded U: at least 30% of the cup's bars have lows in its bottom quarter.

facts.quote: At most two weeks inside the cup with a high-to-low range of 10% or more.
facts.claim: At most two weeks with a 10% or wider range inside the cup.

facts.quote: The right side climbs back to within about 10% of the left-side high before the handle starts.
facts.claim: The right side climbs back within about 10% of the left-side high before the handle.

facts.quote: The handle is at least 5 sessions long.
facts.claim: The handle is at least 5 sessions long.

facts.quote: The handle's midpoint (halfway between its high and low) sits above the cup's midpoint.
facts.claim: The handle's midpoint sits above the cup's midpoint.

facts.quote: The handle's lows drift sideways to down: a straight line fitted through the handle's daily lows slopes flat or down. Rising lows (a wedge) is not a handle.
facts.claim: The handle's lows drift sideways to down; rising lows are a wedge, not a handle.

facts.quote: The handle's average daily volume is below the cup's average daily volume.
facts.claim: The handle's volume averages below the cup's.

facts.quote: The handle holds above the 50-day line: no daily close below the 50-day SMA during the handle.
facts.claim: No daily close below the 50-day during the handle.

facts.quote: Tight at the end: the last 5 handle closes sit within about 3% of each other.
facts.claim: Tight at the end: the last 5 handle closes within about 3% of each other.

facts.quote: A few cents under the low of the buy day, or of the prior day.
facts.claim: The stop: a few cents under the buy day's low or the prior day's low.

facts.quote: Never wider than a few cents under the handle low: below the handle low the setup has failed. IBD's 7% to 8% loss limit is a reference, not ours.
facts.claim: Never wider than a few cents under the handle low; IBD's 7% to 8% is not ours.

facts.quote: 62% of cup breakouts come back to the breakout price within 30 days (Bulkowski). The day's-low stop will be tested often; that is normal, not a reason to widen it.
facts.claim: 62% of cup breakouts come back to the breakout price within 30 days; the stop is tested, not widened.

facts.quote: After the buy, a close back into the handle is a warning, not an exit by itself.
facts.claim: A close back into the handle is a warning, not an exit.

facts.quote: First or second base since the last real correction; a third or later base is graded down.
facts.claim: First or second base; a third or later is graded down.

facts.quote: Before the buy: the cup is a V, or deeper than 35% outside a bear market.
facts.claim: A V, or deeper than 35% outside a bear market, ends the setup.

facts.quote: Before the buy: the handle runs past about 6 weeks (30 sessions) with no breakout; the base is getting stale.
facts.claim: A handle past about 30 sessions with no breakout is stale.

facts.quote: Before the buy: volume rises through the handle.
facts.claim: Volume rising through the handle ends the setup.

facts.quote: Before the buy: a close below the 50-day during the handle.
facts.claim: A close below the 50-day during the handle ends the setup.

facts.quote: Before the buy: the handle's lows rise (wedging), or the handle is shorter than 5 days.
facts.claim: Rising handle lows, or a handle under 5 days, end the setup.

facts.quote: Up to 50% deep only for a cup formed in a bear market.
facts.claim: Up to 50% deep only in a bear market.

facts.quote: The cup falls no more than about 2.5 times the index's decline over the same weeks.
facts.claim: The cup falls no more than about 2.5 times the index's decline.

facts.quote: A cue, not a rule: best at the start of a new market uptrend after a correction, with the group leading and several of its stocks setting up.
facts.claim: Best at the start of a new uptrend, with the group leading.

facts.quote: A flat base falls 15% or less and stays boxy with a flat ceiling tapped at least twice; a cup falls 12% to 33% in a rounded U and then dips again into a handle before the buy.
facts.claim: A flat base stays boxy; a cup is a deeper rounded U followed by a handle.

facts.quote: A cup is one rounded decline whose right side climbs back within 10% of the old high, then one handle at the rim; a VCP shows two or more separate pullbacks, each smaller than the last
facts.claim: A cup is one rounded decline and one handle; a VCP is two or more shrinking pullbacks.

facts.quote: pauses 5 to 30 sessions with no rounded decline; a cup follows a 30% run and takes at least 7 weeks to round out and handle.
facts.claim: A high tight flag pauses with no rounded decline; a cup follows a 30% run and takes 7 weeks or more.

facts.quote: Calling a 2 or 3-day dip a handle; under 5 days it is not one.
facts.claim: A named mistake: calling a 2 or 3-day dip a handle.

facts.quote: Treating the measured-move target as a sure thing; Bulkowski found only 61% reach it.
facts.claim: A named mistake: treating the measured-move target as a sure thing.

facts.quote: ch.handle_volume: dries up sharply
facts.claim: The A+ handle volume dries up sharply.

facts.quote: ch.shape_no_wild_weeks: jagged, V-ish, two violent weeks inside (ULTA)
facts.claim: A jagged cup with violent weeks inside is a B- cue.

facts.quote: ch.base_count: third or later
facts.claim: A third or later base is a B- cue.

facts.quote: A handle in the upper third of the base, within about 5% of the old high, is better.
facts.claim: A handle in the upper third, within about 5% of the old high, is better.

facts.quote: Best between 3 and 6 months (63 to 126 sessions), symmetric; very long or lopsided cups grade down.
facts.claim: Cups are best between 3 and 6 months long.

facts.quote: A wedging or deep handle, a V-shaped cup or a late base breaks out and fades back through the pivot to the stop.
facts.claim: The failure mode: a bad handle, a V or a late base fades back through the pivot to the stop.

facts.quote: A very tight trigger-day stop is cheap but fragile; the house answer is the breakeven move at 2R to 5R (B19), not a wider stop.
facts.claim: BX: a very tight stop is fragile; the answer is breakeven at 2R to 5R, not a wider stop.

facts.quote: A cup over 6 months old with the handle resting on the 50-day is a late, tired base; the base-count rule is the filter the scan cannot apply.
facts.claim: WDAY: a cup over 6 months old with the handle on the 50-day is a late, tired base.

facts.quote: Before the buy: the market reading turns Red.
facts.claim: A Red reading before the buy ends the setup.

facts.quote: Never move the stop closer to make it fit.
facts.claim: Never move the stop closer to make the size fit.

facts.quote: ch.handle_position: just above the midpoint
facts.claim: A handle just above the cup's midpoint is a B- cue.

facts.claim: ULTA: a mid-range close, a four-day fade to the stop, best 0.91R; a B- base.
BX, trigger 2019-11-26: buy 53.11, stop 52.49 (1.17%); stopped 4 sessions later at a low of 51.78.

facts.claim: BX: a 4.9x breakout reached 2.37R on day two, then one dip took the stop and the stock went on without us.

walkthroughs.title: FFIV, January 2014: the clean one
steps: FFIV, January 2014. After a 40% run, a symmetric cup, 15.6 weeks and 17.5% deep. A rounded U, not a V.
The handle: 7 days, 4.2% deep, volume at 0.74x the cup's. It sits high in the base and drifts down.
2014-01-13: it clears the handle high on 2.71x volume. Buy at market, 91.29. Stop under the day's low, 90.67.
Failure mode: a fade back through the pivot to the stop. Instead it reaches 3R the next day. A third comes off.

walkthroughs.title: MCO, September 2012: the long handle
steps: MCO, 2012. After a 40% run, a 21.6-week cup, 21.3% deep. The long, slow version of the pattern.
The handle runs 19 days and 6.7% deep. Its lows drift down, volume dries to 0.77x, and the 50-day holds.
2012-09-06: it clears the handle high on 1.6x volume. Buy at market, 40.76. Stop under the day's low, 39.73.
Failure mode: a handle that wedges up or sinks too low. This one drifted down and held. 3R in 4 sessions.

walkthroughs.title: AX, January 2026: the trims and the trail
steps: AX, 2026. A 72% run, then a 16.6-week U, 20.2% deep. The handle lasts 5 days, the IBD minimum.
2026-01-05: it clears the handle high on 1.48x volume. Buy at market, 89.22. Stop under the day's low, 86.95.
At 3R a third comes off and the stop goes to breakeven. 5R comes in about 7 weeks: another third.
Failure mode: a fade back through the pivot. AX rolled over below it after 5R. The 21-day trail sells the last third.

questions.q: In one line, what is a cup with handle?
choices: A tight box under a flat ceiling
A rounded U, then a dip near the top
Shrinking pullbacks, one after another
A pause with no rounded decline

wrong.Shrinking pullbacks, one after another: That is a VCP's contractions. A cup is one rounded decline and one handle.
wrong.A tight box under a flat ceiling: That is a flat base. A cup rounds down and back up, then dips into a handle.
wrong.A pause with no rounded decline: That is a high tight flag, which pauses with no rounded decline. A cup rounds down first, then dips into a handle.

questions.answer: A rounded U, then a dip near the top
questions.why: A rounded U, then a dip near the top. IBD: cup-with-handle patterns are shaped like the silhouette of a tea cup viewed from the side. Zanger: the cup is the rest after a powerful advance. Our card adds one handle at the rim after the rounded decline. It is not a flat box, a run of shrinking pullbacks, or a pause with no rounded decline.
questions.lesson_line: A cup is a leader's rounded rest, and the handle is the last quiet dip before the breakout.
questions.simple: A cup with handle is a rounded U after a strong run, then one small dip near the top.

reasons: +1 fixed before (variety rewrite)

questions.q: On our card, which level does price have to trade through to trigger the buy?
choices: The cup's lowest low
The highest price in the handle
The low of the handle's dip
The old high before the cup

wrong.The cup's lowest low: That is the bottom of the cup, the base's floor. The buy is at the top.
wrong.The low of the handle's dip: The handle low is the floor of the last dip, the outer limit for the stop.
wrong.The old high before the cup: Zanger buys as it emerges into new highs at the top of the handle, not at the old high point set some 8 to 12 weeks ago.

questions.answer: The highest price in the handle
questions.why: The highest price in the handle. That level is the pivot. We buy as price trades above it in regular hours, at market. IBD adds 10 cents to it, but with a market order the 10 cents does not matter. Zanger buys at the top of the handle, not at the old high point.
questions.lesson_line: Mark the handle high before the open. That is the pivot.
questions.simple: We buy when price trades through the highest price in the handle. That level is the pivot.

reasons: +2 rests on held decision D-003 (the 10 cents offset)
+1 fixed before (variety rewrite)

questions.q: On a cup breakout, the stop sits a few cents under the cup's lowest low.
questions.why: False. The stop sits a few cents under the buy day's low or the prior day's low, not exactly on it. Stop first, then the size comes from the stop. The cup's lowest low is far wider than that, and if the honest stop does not fit the risk, we skip the trade.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first: a few cents under the day's low.
questions.simple: False. The stop goes a few cents under the day's low, not the cup's low, which is far too wide.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (A3, F62)
+1 fixed before (variety rewrite)

questions.q: A sharp V-shaped drop and rebound still counts as a cup if the depth is right.
questions.why: False. A cup must be a rounded U, and a V fails even when the depth fits. IBD: V-shaped patterns are less reliable. StockCharts: a V-shaped bottom is too sharp of a reversal to qualify. Our card needs at least 30% of the cup's bars to have their low in the cup's bottom quarter.
questions.lesson_line: A cup is rounded. A V is a fast round trip, not a rest.
questions.simple: False. A V is too sharp and quick to be a cup, even when the depth is right.

deeper.trap: A V and a U can fall the same amount. The difference is time at the bottom. Our card wants at least 30% of the cup's bars to have lows in its bottom quarter. A V drops, turns and climbs straight back, so it spends too few bars down there.

reasons: stable definition, IBD and StockCharts agree

questions.q: Tap the number that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: A handle must last a minimum of ___ sessions to count as one.
questions.why: 5. A handle needs a minimum of 5 sessions. IBD: if it's shorter than five days, it's not a handle. IBD also says handles must be at least five days long.
questions.lesson_line: Five sessions or it is not a handle. Count them.
questions.simple: A handle needs a minimum of 5 sessions. Under five days it is not a handle.

reasons: stable definition, IBD states it twice

questions.q: Where in the base should the handle form?
choices: In the upper half of the whole base
Near the cup's lowest low in the base
Centered right on the cup's midpoint
Just below the 50-day average line

wrong.Near the cup's lowest low in the base: That is the lower half of the cup, and the handle should not extend there. Handles that form too low fail more often.
wrong.Centered right on the cup's midpoint: Half of it would sit in the lower half. The handle's midpoint has to sit above the cup's midpoint, not on it.
wrong.Just below the 50-day average line: A handle generally forms above the 50-day line, not under it.

questions.answer: In the upper half of the whole base
questions.why: In the upper half of the base. IBD: a proper handle forms in the upper half of a base and drifts slightly downward along its price lows. Bulkowski says the same, and AAII says the handle should not extend into the lower half of the cup. Our card tests it with midpoints: the handle's midpoint must sit above the cup's midpoint. IBD adds that handles that form too low present added risk of failure.
questions.lesson_line: The handle forms high in the base, in its upper half.
questions.simple: The handle forms in the upper half of the base. A handle that forms too low fails more often.

reasons: IBD, Bulkowski and AAII agree

questions.q: On our card, the handle's average daily volume runs below the cup's average daily volume.
questions.why: True. The handle's average daily volume is below the cup's average daily volume. IBD: volume should dry up, evidence that the weak holders are just about gone, and it should mostly ease until the breakout. Quiet trading in the handle suggests few holders are still selling. Volume that rises through the handle ends the setup before the buy.
questions.lesson_line: Quiet in the handle is a sign the sellers are running out.
questions.simple: True. Handle trading is quieter than the cup's, a sign the sellers are running out.

reasons: IBD and the card agree

questions.q: The handle high is 48.20. On our breakout rule, when do you buy?
choices: On a daily close above the right rim
In premarket, if it gaps over 48.20
On a regular-hours trade over 48.20
At the handle low, before the move

wrong.On a daily close above the right rim: That is Bulkowski's later entry. We buy the trade through the handle high.
wrong.In premarket, if it gaps over 48.20: No new buys outside regular trading hours.
wrong.At the handle low, before the move: That is before the breakout. Our breakout rule waits for price to trade through the handle high.

questions.why: On a regular-hours trade through 48.20, at market. Our trigger is the trade through the pivot, the handle's highest price. Bulkowski waits for a close above the right cup rim, a later entry that we do not use. No new buys outside regular hours, so a premarket gap does not count. Buying at the handle low comes before the breakout.
questions.lesson_line: The trigger is the trade through the handle high. Market order, regular hours.
questions.simple: We buy as price trades through 48.20 in regular hours, with a market order, not on a close or in premarket.

deeper.counter: Two published entries differ. Bulkowski buys when price closes above the right cup rim. Zanger buys as it emerges into new highs at the top of the handle, not at the old high point. We use the second kind of entry: the trade through the handle high, at market, in regular hours.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (E57, E58)
+1 fixed before (variety rewrite)

questions.q: Tap the number that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: The shortest a cup with handle can be is ___ weeks, the handle included.
questions.why: 7 weeks. IBD: the base must be at least seven weeks long, including the handle. Our card counts 35 sessions from the left-side high to the day before the breakout. Bulkowski's range starts at 7 weeks too.
questions.lesson_line: Seven weeks or more. A real cup takes time to build.
questions.simple: The shortest cup with handle is 7 weeks, and the handle counts toward that time.

reasons: IBD and Bulkowski agree

questions.q: IBD wants a run up of no more than 30% before the stock turns down into the cup.
questions.why: False. IBD: the pattern's basic requirements start with a run up of at least 30% before the stock turns down into a consolidation. AAII also asks for at least 30% from the last intermediate low. Our card measures the rise from the lowest low of the prior 6 months, 120 sessions, to the left-side high.
questions.lesson_line: No run, no cup. Measure the advance before the rest.
questions.simple: False. IBD wants a run up of at least 30% first, not at most, so no strong run means no cup.

reasons: +1 fixed before (variety rewrite)

questions.q: A handle's lows rise day after day into the pivot, with no shakeout. What kind of handle is that?
choices: A handle that wedges up
A handle that runs sideways
A handle that drifts down
A handle with a shakeout

wrong.A handle that drifts down: Drifting means the lows slope sideways to down. Rising lows are the opposite.
wrong.A handle that runs sideways: Sideways means the lows stay level. These lows rise day after day, which is a wedge.
wrong.A handle with a shakeout: The story says there is no shakeout here. The lows only climb.

questions.why: A handle that wedges up. IBD: a wedging handle with no shakeouts is a sign to steer clear. Overeager handles that wedge upward tend to fail, while handles that drift lower foreshadow assertive action. Our card says the handle's lows drift sideways to down, and rising lows are not a handle.
questions.lesson_line: A handle drifts down or sideways. Rising lows into the pivot are a wedge.
questions.simple: Rising lows with no shakeout make a wedging handle. IBD says steer clear, because wedging handles tend to fail.

deeper.trap: A wedge can look like strength, because the stock holds up and the lows climb. That is the trap. IBD reads it the other way: handles that wedge upward tend to fail, while handles that drift lower foreshadow assertive action.

reasons: IBD states it in two articles

questions.q: On our card, one daily close under the 50-day during the handle ends the setup.
questions.why: True. A close below the 50-day during the handle ends the setup on our card: the handle holds above the 50-day with no daily close below it. IBD is looser, saying a handle should generally form above the 50-day. The one-close test is our card's line.
questions.lesson_line: The handle holds the 50-day on every close. One close under it and the cup is off.
questions.simple: True. On our card, one close under the 50-day during the handle ends the setup.

reasons: +2 the one-close test is a proposed card line, listed in the lesson conflicts

questions.q: How far below the left-side high may the right side stop before the handle starts, on our card?
choices: About 10% below it, at most
About 20% below, at most
About 30% below, at most
It must hit the old high

wrong.About 30% below, at most: Far too loose. A right side that stops well short leaves the handle low in the base, and low handles fail more.
wrong.It must hit the old high: Zanger puts the handle about 5% below the old high, so the right side does not have to reach it.
wrong.About 20% below, at most: Too loose. Our card wants the right side back within about 10% of the left-side high.

questions.why: About 10% below it, at most. Our card has the right side climb back to within about 10% of the left-side high before the handle starts. Only then can the handle sit high in the base. Zanger puts the handle about 5% below the old high and calls a lower one riskier.
questions.lesson_line: The right side comes back up near the old high. Only then does a handle start.
questions.simple: The right side should climb back to within about 10% of the left-side high before the handle starts.

reasons: +1 fixed before (why rewritten by the checker)

questions.q: In Bulkowski's bull-market results, few cup breakouts come back to the breakout price.
questions.why: False. In Bulkowski's bull-market results, the throwback rate is 62%: most cup breakouts come back to the breakout price. A retest is the usual case, not the rare one.
questions.lesson_line: Expect the retest. Most cup breakouts come back to the breakout price.
questions.simple: False. In Bulkowski's bull-market results, 62% of cup breakouts come back to the breakout price.

deeper.counter: A pullback to the pivot is not a failure. In Bulkowski's bull-market results, 62% of cup breakouts come back to the breakout price. Do not read the scare as a verdict. The stop decides whether the trade is over.

reasons: +3 one cited fact only (Bulkowski)
+2 a measured statistic that Bulkowski updates
+1 fixed before (variety rewrite)

questions.q: What is the widest our cup stop can ever sit?
choices: 8% under the buy price
A few cents under the cup's low
Just under the handle low
Under the 200-day average

wrong.A few cents under the cup's low: That is the whole cup's depth away. Far too wide.
wrong.8% under the buy price: IBD's 7% to 8% is a reference, not ours.
wrong.Under the 200-day average: The 200-day decides whether we may buy a long at all, not where the stop sits.

questions.why: Just under the handle low, by a few cents. That is the outer wall. Below the handle low the setup has failed, so a wider stop is never allowed. The real stop usually sits much closer, a few cents under the day's low and within about 3% of the buy. Bulkowski also puts his stop at the handle low. IBD's 7% to 8% loss limit is a reference, not ours.
questions.lesson_line: The handle low is the outer wall. The real stop usually sits much closer.
questions.simple: The stop can never sit wider than a few cents under the handle low, because below it the setup has failed.

deeper.trap: The handle low is a limit, not a target. Pick the stop first: a few cents under the day's low or the prior day's low. If that honest stop does not fit the risk, skip the trade. Never pull the stop closer to make the size fit, and never push it past the handle low to buy more room.

reasons: +2 the outer limit is a proposed card line (ch.stop_outer_limit)
+1 fixed before (variety rewrite)

questions.q: On our card, a third or later base since the last real correction is graded down.
questions.why: True. Our card takes a first or second base since the last real correction and grades a third or later one down. IBD: it's usually best to buy a first-stage or second-stage base, and breakouts from late-stage bases will often blow up. Graded down does not mean banned.
questions.lesson_line: Count the bases. A late one gets a lower grade.
questions.simple: True. Our card grades a third or later base down, because late-stage breakouts often blow up.

reasons: +2 rests on a proposed card line that conflicts with the SET.07 pilot (lesson conflicts)

questions.q: How many weeks with a 10% or wider range can a cup hold inside it, on our card?
choices: None at all
At most two
At most three
At most five

wrong.None at all: The card allows up to two. More than that is too jagged.
wrong.At most five: Five wild weeks is a jagged base. IBD wants smooth sides.
wrong.At most three: Three wild weeks is already too jagged. The card allows two.

questions.why: At most two. Our card allows at most two weeks inside the cup with a high-to-low range of 10% or more. IBD wants smooth action on both sides, with no jagged edges and not many wild weekly swings of 10% to 15% or more. A U shape alone is not enough, because smoothness is its own test.
questions.lesson_line: A cup is smooth. Count the violent weeks; more than two and it is not ours.
questions.simple: A cup can hold at most two weeks with a 10% or wider range. More wild weeks make it too jagged.

reasons: IBD and the card agree

questions.q: One R is the fill minus the stop. Fill 38.60, stop 37.90. By our hard rule, at what price does the first third come off?
questions.why: 40.70, the 3R level. One R is the fill minus the stop. Add three of those to the fill and you get 40.70. The hard rule is a third off at 3R. Another third comes off at 5R and the last third trails.
questions.lesson_line: Know your 3R before the open. A third comes off there.
questions.simple: By our hard rule a third comes off at 3R, which is the fill plus three times the gap down to the stop.

reasons: a computed key (38.60 + 3 x 0.70)
rests on the owner's rulebook B19: the hard rule is a third at 3R
the stem says hard rule because the owner's practice is to wait longer

questions.q: Our card lets a cup fall up to about 2.5 times the index's decline over the same weeks.
questions.why: True. Our card says the cup falls no more than about 2.5 times the index's decline over the same weeks. IBD quotes O'Neil that growth stocks correct 1-1/2 to 2-1/2 times the market averages. So a leader falls more than the index, but not wildly more.
questions.lesson_line: Measure the cup against the market. A leader falls more than the index, but not wildly more.
questions.simple: True. A leader falls more than the index in a cup, but our card caps it at about 2.5 times.

reasons: the card and IBD agree

questions.q: IBD allows a cup to run as deep as 50% when it forms in a bear market.
questions.why: True. IBD: in bear markets, cups can run as deep as 50%. Our card allows that depth only for a cup formed in a bear market.
questions.lesson_line: A deep cup is allowed only when the whole market fell hard.
questions.simple: True. A cup can run as deep as 50% in a bear market, and our card allows that depth only then.

reasons: IBD and the card agree

questions.q: Before the buy, volume drying up through the handle ends the setup.
questions.why: False. Volume rising through the handle ends the setup. Drying up is what we want. IBD: volume should dry up, evidence that the weak holders are just about gone, and it should mostly ease until the breakout.
questions.lesson_line: A loud handle means sellers are still there. Wait for quiet.
questions.simple: False. A handle that dries up is the good sign, and volume rising through the handle is what ends the setup.

reasons: +1 fixed before (variety rewrite)

questions.q: IBD says many cups take how long to form?
choices: Four to six weeks
Three to six months
Two to three years
About seven weeks

wrong.Two to three years: IBD's longest is 65 weeks, a bit over a year.
wrong.Four to six weeks: That is under the seven-week minimum for a cup. A flat base can be as short as five weeks.
wrong.About seven weeks: Seven weeks is the minimum, not the typical length.

questions.why: Three to six months. IBD: cups range from seven weeks to as long as 65 weeks, with many forming over three to six months. Seven weeks is the minimum, not the usual length. Our card grades 3 to 6 months (63 to 126 sessions) best, and very long or lopsided cups grade down.
questions.lesson_line: A real base builds slowly. Months, not days.
questions.simple: IBD says many cups form over three to six months, and they can run from seven weeks up to 65 weeks.

reasons: +2 touches held decision D-051 (the 65-week maximum is not keyed)

questions.q: Buy the breakout today?
questions.story: The handle is tight and quiet. The pivot trades through this morning. Earnings come out after tomorrow's close.
choices: Buy it; the pivot just triggered
Buy half size and keep the stop
Pass; earnings are inside 3 days
Pass; buy at tomorrow's close instead

wrong.Buy it; the pivot just triggered: The trigger fired, and the calendar still says no. No new buys in the 3 days before a report.
wrong.Buy half size and keep the stop: Smaller is still a new buy. The rule is no new buys.
wrong.Pass; buy at tomorrow's close instead: Tomorrow's close is still before the report. That buy lands inside the 3 days, so the rule still says no.

questions.why: Skip it. No new buys in the 3 days before an earnings report, and this report comes after tomorrow's close. The trigger firing does not override the calendar, and a smaller size does not either. Waiting for tomorrow's close does not help, because that buy still lands before the report.
questions.lesson_line: No new buys in the 3 days before earnings. The calendar beats the trigger.
questions.simple: Skip it. We take no new buys in the 3 days before an earnings report, even when the pivot triggers.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (B22)
+1 fixed before (variety rewrite)

questions.q: Lowest low of the prior six months 30.00, left-side high 40.50. How big was the run into the cup, in percent?
questions.why: 35%. The rise from the lowest low of 30.00 to the left-side high of 40.50, divided by 30.00, is 35%. A cup needs a run of at least 30% before it. IBD says so, and AAII also asks for at least 30%.
questions.lesson_line: Measure the run before the rest. A cup with no run in front of it is just a dip.
questions.simple: The stock rose 35% from its low to the high, which clears the 30% a cup needs after a run.

deeper.counter: The 30% is common ground, but AAII repeats O'Neil, so IBD and AAII are one view, not two. They differ on the start. AAII counts from the last intermediate low. Our card counts from the lowest low of the prior 6 months.

reasons: a computed key

questions.q: Left-side high 80.00, the cup's lowest intraday low 58.00. How deep is the cup, in percent?
questions.why: 27.5%. Depth is the fall from the left-side high to the cup's low, divided by the 80.00 high. IBD measures the decline from the stock's high. Zanger measures it off the old high point. Dividing by the low would measure from the wrong place.
questions.lesson_line: Depth is high to low, divided by the high. Measure it; do not eyeball it.
questions.simple: The cup is 27.5% deep because we divide the drop from the high to the low by the high.

reasons: a computed key
tied to the held cup-depth decision D-052

questions.q: Left-side high 62.00, cup low 44.00. Where is the cup's midpoint?
questions.why: 53.00, halfway between the left-side high 62.00 and the cup low 44.00. The gap between them is the cup's height, not its midpoint. IBD: the midpoint of the handle's high and low should be above the midpoint of the cup. Our card uses the same test.
questions.lesson_line: Find the cup's midpoint first. The handle has to sit above it.
questions.simple: The midpoint is 53.00, halfway between 62.00 and 44.00, and the handle's own midpoint must sit above it.

reasons: a computed key

questions.q: Take the breakout when it comes?
questions.story: Left-side high 60.00, cup low 44.00. The right side climbs back near 59. Then a six-session handle runs from 57.00 down to 45.00.
choices: Take it; the handle is long enough
Pass; the handle sits too low
Take it; the right side made it back
Wait for the handle to recover

wrong.Take it; the handle is long enough: Length is one test. Position is another, and it fails.
wrong.Take it; the right side made it back: The right side did. Then the handle fell too far.
wrong.Wait for the handle to recover: The handle's low of 45.00 already sits under the halfway point between 60.00 and 44.00, in the cup's lower half. AAII: the handle should not extend into the lower half, and a rally cannot undo that low.

questions.answer: Pass; the handle sits too low
questions.why: Pass. The handle's midpoint, halfway between 57.00 and 45.00, sits under the cup's midpoint, halfway between 60.00 and 44.00. A handle in that spot ends the setup before the buy. IBD: handles that form too low present added risk of failure during breakouts. AAII agrees: the handle should not extend into the lower half of the cup. The right side did climb back near the old high, but that is a separate test.
questions.lesson_line: Check the handle's midpoint against the cup's. Too low and I pass.
questions.simple: Pass. The handle's midpoint sits below the cup's midpoint, so the handle formed too low.

reasons: +2 computed key (the two midpoints)

questions.q: Fill 56.61, stop 55.27. How far below the fill is the stop, in percent, to two decimals?
questions.why: 2.37%. Take the gap between the fill and the stop, then divide it by the fill, 56.61. Our stop usually sits within about 3% of the buy, so this fits. These are GWW's numbers from 2004-09-29, where the stop was 2.4%.
questions.lesson_line: Measure the stop in percent of the fill. About 3% or less is our usual.
questions.simple: The stop is 2.37% below the fill, found by dividing the gap to the stop by the fill, inside the usual 3%.

reasons: a computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook and the held stop-width decision D-008

questions.q: What is the most you may pay for it?
questions.story: We never pay more than 4% over the handle high. The handle high is 60.00. You were away for the open. At 10:30 the stock trades 62.70.

wrong.$60.10: That is the handle high plus IBD's 10 cents. Our limit is 4% over the handle high.
wrong.$62.70: That is today's price, and it is past the 4% line.
wrong.$63.00: That is past the 4% line too.

questions.why: 62.40. We never buy more than 4% above the buy point, and 4% over the 60.00 handle high is 62.40. At 62.70 the stock is past that line, so we pass. Chasing also costs size: the stop stays put, so the distance grows and the shares shrink.
questions.lesson_line: I would rather miss it than chase it. Four percent and done.
questions.simple: The most we may pay is 4% over the 60.00 handle high, which is 62.40. The stock is at 62.70, so we pass.

deeper.trap: The 4% line is measured from the buy point, here the handle high of 60.00. At 62.70 the stock is already past it, so we pass. A late entry keeps the same stop, so the distance grows and the shares shrink.

reasons: a computed key (60.00 x 1.04)
rests on the owner's rulebook C28: the 4% chase line, stated in the story

questions.q: What do you do?
questions.story: Four days after the breakout at 40.76, price slips back to the handle high. Your stop is 39.73.
choices: Hold; the stop stays where it is
Widen the stop to the handle low
Sell now; the breakout has failed
Move the stop up to breakeven

wrong.Widen the stop to the handle low: Never wider. The gap rule is the one exception, and this is not a gap.
wrong.Sell now; the breakout has failed: A pullback to the pivot is not a failure. The stop decides.
wrong.Move the stop up to breakeven: Breakeven comes between 2R and 5R, not on a slide to the pivot.

questions.answer: Hold; the stop stays where it is
questions.why: Hold it, with the stop at 39.73. The stop only moves up, never down or wider, apart from the gap rule. A pullback toward the pivot is common: Bulkowski found 62% of cup breakouts come back to the breakout price within 30 days. Selling because it dipped throws away the plan, since the stop is the exit. Breakeven comes only between 2R and 5R.
questions.lesson_line: The retest is normal. The stop pays for it; you do not widen it.
questions.simple: Hold the stop where it is. Tests of the breakout price are normal, and the stop only moves up.

deeper.trap: Two moves feel safe and are wrong. Widening the stop breaks the rule that a stop never moves down or wider, and the gap rule is the only exception. Moving it to breakeven early skips the 2R to 5R window. A dip back to the pivot is a normal test, not a verdict.

reasons: +2 the story reuses dossier numbers the owner has not reviewed (D-007) on top of the rulebook (A4)
+2 a measured statistic that Bulkowski updates

questions.q: What now?
questions.story: You bought the breakout at 91.20 with the stop at 89.10. The handle low is 88.40. It closes at 89.60, back inside the handle.
choices: Sell at the close; it failed
Hold; the stop is still the exit
Lower the stop to handle low
Add; the price is cheaper

wrong.Lower the stop to handle low: The stop only moves up, never down.
wrong.Sell at the close; it failed: That close is a warning, not an exit by itself. The stop decides.
wrong.Add; the price is cheaper: Full size at one price with one stop. No adding.

questions.answer: Hold; the stop is still the exit
questions.why: Hold it. A close back into the handle is a warning, not an exit by itself. The stop is the exit, and it was set before the buy at 89.10. It only moves up, never down. The close at 89.60 is above the stop, so the plan is still on. Adding is out too: it is the full size at one price with one stop.
questions.lesson_line: A weak close is a warning. The stop is the decision.
questions.simple: Hold. A close back inside the handle is a warning, not an exit, and the stop you set before the buy decides.

deeper.trap: Two reflexes follow a weak close: selling by feel and adding because it is cheaper. The plan has no rule for either. Wait for the stop. If it fills, take the loss and move on, and buy again only if the setup triggers again, as a new trade with its own stop.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (A4, A5)
+1 fixed before (variety rewrite)

questions.q: Where is the stop now?
questions.story: You bought at 54.57 with the stop at 52.94. It gaps open at 52.40, under your stop. The first 30-minute bar's low is 52.10.
choices: Sell at the open, at 52.40
52.10, the first 30-minute low
No stop until it reclaims 52.94
Get out; the gap is past 2R

wrong.No stop until it reclaims 52.94: There is always a stop. The new one is the 30-minute low.
wrong.Get out; the gap is past 2R: The 30-minute low is inside 2R here. The ceiling has not been hit.
wrong.Sell at the open, at 52.40: The gap rule gives it the first 30 minutes. The 30-minute low decides.

questions.why: 52.10, the first 30-minute bar's low. A gap through the stop is the one exception to a stop that only moves up. The first 30 minutes of the gap-down day decide, and that bar's low is the new stop. The ceiling is 2R: if the first 30 minutes take the loss past 2R, get out. Here the loss at 52.10 stays inside 2R, so the ceiling is not hit.
questions.lesson_line: A gap through the stop is the one exception. The first 30 minutes decide.
questions.simple: On a gap through the stop, the first 30-minute bar's low is the new stop. This loss stays inside 2R.

deeper.trap: The gap rule is the only time a stop may move down. It is not 'no stop' and it is not 'sell at the open'. Wait for the first 30-minute bar and use its low as the new stop. Get out at once only if those 30 minutes take the loss past 2R.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B20 gap rule with the 2R ceiling)
the 'inside 2R' test is computed from the story (loss 2.47 against one R of 1.63)

questions.q: Bought at 72.40, stop 71.60. On day two it trades 74.40. How many R is that?
questions.why: 2.5R. The gain per share divided by the risk per share, the fill minus the stop, is 2.5. The first trim waits for 3R, and the stop only moves up.
questions.lesson_line: Count in R: the gain per share over the risk per share.
questions.simple: The gain per share divided by the risk per share is 2.5R.

deeper.trap: R is the gain per share divided by the risk per share, not a percent of the fill. At 2.5R the first trim has not come yet, because the hard rule is a third at 3R. The stop still only moves up, never down or wider.

reasons: a computed key (2.00 / 0.80)
rests on the owner's rulebook B19 and A4; the item only counts R and keys no action

questions.q: Account 40,000. Risk 0.75%. Fill 40.76, stop 39.73. How many shares, before any cap?
questions.why: 291. Risk dollars are the account times the risk percent. Divide them by the fill minus the stop and round down to 291. The cap comes after, and the smaller number wins. The stop sets the size, never the other way round.
questions.lesson_line: The stop sets the size. Round down.
questions.simple: Dividing the risk dollars by the gap between fill and stop, then rounding down, gives 291 shares.

reasons: a computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook (A5)

questions.q: Take the breakout?
questions.story: A 13-week, 20% cup. Then six days of rising lows into the pivot, and no shakeout.
choices: Take it; the cup is the right depth
Pass; a wedging handle
Take it; rising lows show strength

wrong.Take it; the cup is the right depth: The cup passes. The handle is what fails.
wrong.Take it; rising lows show strength: IBD: handles that wedge upward tend to fail.

questions.why: Pass. Rising handle lows are a wedge, not a handle. IBD: a wedging handle with no shakeouts is a sign to steer clear. This one was stopped at 0.0R.
questions.lesson_line: A handle drifts down. Rising lows into the pivot are a wedge, and I pass.

questions.q: Is it a cup with handle?
questions.story: After a 64% run the stock dips and recovers over four weeks. Then it rests seven days just under the high.
choices: Yes; the handle is long enough
No; too few weeks to be a cup
Yes; the run before it qualifies
No; the run is too big for a cup

wrong.Yes; the handle is long enough: The handle passes. The cup is too short.
wrong.Yes; the run before it qualifies: The run qualifies. The time does not.
wrong.No; the run is too big for a cup: IBD asks for a run of at least 30%, so 64% is plenty. The problem is the time, not the run.

questions.answer: No; too few weeks to be a cup
questions.why: No. A cup spans at least 7 weeks, the handle included. Four weeks of dip and recovery plus a seven-day rest still falls short. It is a flag or a short base at best. The 64% run is fine: IBD wants a run of at least 30%. The time is what fails.
questions.lesson_line: Count the weeks before you call it a cup. A short dip and a pause is a flag.
questions.simple: A cup needs at least 7 weeks, handle included, and this one is shorter, so it is not a cup.

reasons: story built from the unreviewed dossier example d29 (D-007)
7-week floor is stated by IBD, Bulkowski and our card

questions.q: What is it?
questions.story: An 8.4-week rest that dips only 6.6% from the high. Then a 9-day handle, and a breakout on heavy volume.
choices: A flat base with a late dip
A shallow cup and handle
A VCP of shrinking dips
Not a base; no real dip

wrong.A VCP of shrinking dips: A VCP shows two or more separate shrinking pullbacks. This is one shallow shelf.
wrong.A shallow cup and handle: A cup is a deeper rounded U. A 6.6% dip is only a shelf.
wrong.Not a base; no real dip: A flat base falls 15% or less, and a shelf this shallow fits that. It is a base, just a shallow one.

questions.answer: A flat base with a late dip
questions.why: A flat base. A flat base falls 15% or less, and a 6.6% dip sits well inside that. A cup is a deeper rounded U followed by a handle. This reads as a flat base, not a cup, even though it ends in a 9-day dip.
questions.lesson_line: Measure the depth first. A shallow shelf is a flat base, whatever the dip at the end looks like.
questions.simple: A dip of only 6.6% is a shallow shelf, so it reads as a flat base, not a cup.

reasons: story built from the unreviewed dossier example d28 (D-007)

questions.q: Take it as a cup with handle?
questions.story: An 11-week cup falls 22% in a straight line and climbs straight back to the high. Then a 5-day handle.
choices: Take it; 22% is a normal depth
Take it; the handle is 5 days
Pass; the cup is a V, not a U
Pass; 22% is too deep for a cup

wrong.Take it; 22% is a normal depth: The depth passes. The shape fails.
wrong.Take it; the handle is 5 days: The handle is long enough, but it sits on a V.
wrong.Pass; 22% is too deep for a cup: IBD puts a cup's decline between 12% and 33%, so 22% is a normal depth. The shape is what fails.

questions.answer: Pass; the cup is a V, not a U
questions.why: Pass. That is a V, not a U. Only 12% of the cup's bars had lows in the bottom quarter, and the card needs 30%. The 22% depth and the 5-day handle both pass, but they cannot fix the shape. IBD: V-shaped patterns are less reliable.
questions.lesson_line: A cup spends time at the bottom. A straight drop and a straight climb is a V.
questions.simple: A cup should round out at the bottom, but this one fell and climbed straight back, which makes it a V.

deeper.trap: Depth and handle length both pass here, so it is easy to wave it through. The shape is a separate test: at least 30% of the cup's bars with lows in the bottom quarter. This cup had 12%. StockCharts agrees that a V-shaped bottom is too sharp a reversal to qualify.

reasons: story built from the unreviewed dossier example d31 and d32 (D-007)
fixed before (a long sentence in the explanation was split)

questions.q: Does the cup with handle name apply yet?
questions.story: After a nine-week rounded base, the stock dips three days just under the rim.
choices: Yes; 3 sessions is enough
Not yet; the dip is too short
Yes; any dip at the rim
Not yet; base is too short

wrong.Not yet; base is too short: A cup spans at least 7 weeks, and a nine-week base is long enough. The shortfall is in the handle.
wrong.Yes; 3 sessions is enough: A handle needs at least five sessions. A three-day dip is not one yet.
wrong.Yes; any dip at the rim: Any dip is not a handle. Five sessions is the floor.

questions.answer: Not yet; the dip is too short
questions.why: Not yet. A handle must last at least 5 sessions. IBD: if it's shorter than five days, it's not a handle. Calling a 2 or 3-day dip a handle is a named mistake. Keep watching. A dip that reaches 5 sessions in the upper half of the base and holds the 50-day can still become a handle.
questions.lesson_line: Count the handle's days. Under five, keep waiting.
questions.simple: A handle must last at least 5 sessions, and a three-day dip is too short, so the name does not apply yet.

reasons: stable rule: IBD and our card agree on the 5-session floor

questions.q: Which handle grades higher?
questions.story: Two cups, both clean. In one, handle volume shrinks to a fraction of the cup's. In the other, it runs 0.97x the cup's average.
choices: The cup with the quieter handle
The cup with the 0.97x handle
Equal; both are below the cup
Neither; both fail the volume gate

wrong.Equal; both are below the cup: Both pass the gate. Grading is about how quiet.
wrong.The cup with the 0.97x handle: It passes, but only just. It is the weakest acceptable.
wrong.Neither; both fail the volume gate: The gate is only that the handle averages below the cup's volume. A 0.97x handle is below it, so both pass.

questions.answer: The cup with the quieter handle
questions.why: The quieter one. Both handles average below the cup's volume, so both pass the gate. Our card reads a sharp dry-up as the A+ cue, and a 0.97x handle as the weakest acceptable. Grading stays a judgment call: the card gives cues, not a fixed checklist.
questions.lesson_line: Quiet passes. Very quiet grades up.
questions.simple: Both pass because both trade quieter than the cup, but the handle that dries up sharply shows the sellers are running out.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook: E50 says grading is discretionary and no fixed checklist is ours
the grade cue is a proposed card row, not a ruling

questions.q: Your read?
questions.story: This is the stock's fourth cup since the last real correction. The shape is clean and the handle is quiet.
choices: A+, the shape is clean
Graded down, sized down
Normal size; base count is ignored
Skip it; late bases are banned

wrong.A+, the shape is clean: Clean shape does not erase the base count.
wrong.Normal size; base count is ignored: Our card counts the bases. Late ones grade down.
wrong.Skip it; late bases are banned: Our card grades a third or later base down. It does not ban it.

questions.why: Graded down, and sized down. Our card grades a third or later base down, and B- or lower setups are sized down. This is the fourth cup since the last real correction. It is not banned, only graded down. IBD: it is usually best to buy a first-stage or second-stage base, and breakouts from late-stage bases will often blow up.
questions.lesson_line: A clean cup late in the run still earns a smaller size.
questions.simple: A late base is graded down and sized down, even when the shape is clean and the handle is quiet.

deeper.trap: The trap is to let a clean chart hide the count. Count the bases since the last real correction before you grade. A first or second base is the best place to buy. A third or later is graded down and sized down, not banned.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (D38, B- sized down)
the base-count row is a proposed card cue and the SET.07 flat-base lesson treats a fourth base differently

questions.q: By our guide, what do you take?
questions.story: Our market reading is Orange. Three cups trigger the same morning. You grade them A+, A and B.
choices: Only the A+ cup; skip the others
The A+ and A cups; skip the B
All three; the B at half size
None of them; stay in cash

wrong.The A+ and A cups; skip the B: Our Orange guide takes only A+ setups. The A cup waits too.
wrong.All three; the B at half size: Our Orange guide takes only A+ setups. The A and B cups wait.
wrong.None of them; stay in cash: Mostly cash is the Red guide. Orange still allows A+ setups.

questions.answer: Only the A+ cup; skip the others
questions.why: Only the A+ cup. Our guide for an Orange reading is A+ setups only, so the A and B cups wait. Green is full risk per grade and up to 10 positions, Yellow is smaller and fewer, and Red is mostly cash and shorts. It is a guide.
questions.lesson_line: Read the market before the cup. In Orange our guide takes A+ setups only.
questions.simple: In an Orange market our guide takes only A+ setups, so the A+ cup is in and the other two wait.

reasons: cites only one fact
rests on the owner's rulebook, read as a guide (F65 under A10)

questions.q: Buy it?
questions.story: The breakout gaps up 3% over the pivot. At your fill the stock sits 12% above its 10-day average.
choices: Buy; it is inside the 4% limit
Skip; too far over the 10-day
Buy half size and keep the stop
Skip; a 3% gap is already chasing

wrong.Buy; it is inside the 4% limit: Inside the chase line, but past the stretch line. Both must pass.
wrong.Buy half size and keep the stop: Size does not fix a stretched entry.
wrong.Skip; a 3% gap is already chasing: The no-chase line is 4% above the buy point, and 3% is inside it. The stretch from the 10-day average is what fails.

questions.why: Skip it. A long more than 10% above its 10-day average is too stretched to buy, even inside the 4% chase line. The fill is only 3% over the pivot, so the first check passes. Both checks must pass, and this one fails the second.
questions.lesson_line: Two checks at the fill: distance from the pivot and distance from the 10-day.
questions.simple: Skip it, since the stock is more than 10% above its 10-day average, even though it is inside the 4% chase limit.

deeper.trap: These are two separate checks. One: never buy more than 4% above the buy point. Two: skip a long that is more than 10% above its 10-day average. Passing the first never excuses failing the second.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C28 and C29, both settled)

questions.q: On our card, is the cup still on your list?
questions.story: In week two of the handle the stock closes under its 50-day once. The next day it recovers above it.
choices: Yes; it recovered the next day
No; it closed under the 50-day
Yes; it takes two closes
No; the handle ran too long

wrong.Yes; it recovered the next day: The recovery does not undo the close. The card's test is one close.
wrong.Yes; it takes two closes: One close under the 50-day in the handle is enough.
wrong.No; the handle ran too long: A handle is usually 1 to 4 weeks, and week two is normal. Length is not the problem.

questions.why: No. On our card, one daily close below the 50-day during the handle ends the setup before the buy, and a recovery the next day does not undo it. IBD says a handle should generally form above the 50-day, and our card turns that into a one-close test. One close is enough, not two.
questions.lesson_line: Inside the handle the 50-day holds every close. One close under and I cross it off.
questions.simple: On our card, one close under the 50-day during the handle ends the setup, even if it bounces back the next day.

reasons: the one-close test is our card's own proposal, while IBD says only 'generally'

questions.q: On our card, a handle is tight at the end when its last 5 closes sit within about 3% of each other.
questions.why: True. Tight at the end means the last 5 handle closes sit within about 3% of each other. IBD asks for areas of tight trading in a handle, and the card gives one way to measure that.
questions.lesson_line: Tight closes into the pivot. That is the picture I want.
questions.simple: True. Our card calls a handle tight when its last 5 closes sit within about 3% of each other.

reasons: a proposed card row, with IBD agreeing on the idea of tight trading

questions.q: Which handle grades higher?
questions.story: Two handles, both above the cup's midpoint. One sits within 5% of the old high. The other sits just above the midpoint.
choices: The handle nearer the old high
The handle just above the midpoint
Equal; both pass the midpoint
Neither; both handles sit too low

wrong.Equal; both pass the midpoint: Both pass. The grade still prefers the higher handle.
wrong.The handle just above the midpoint: It passes the gate, but it is a B- cue.
wrong.Neither; both handles sit too low: Both sit above the cup's midpoint, and one is within 5% of the old high. Zanger puts a good handle about there.

questions.answer: The handle nearer the old high
questions.why: The handle nearer the old high. Both pass the midpoint test, so both are handles. A handle in the upper third, within about 5% of the old high, is better. One just above the midpoint is a B- cue. Zanger: the handle is generally about 5% below the old high, and a lower one is riskier.
questions.lesson_line: Higher in the base is better. Just above halfway passes, and only just.
questions.simple: Both pass the midpoint test. The handle nearer the old high grades higher, and the one just above the midpoint grades lower.

reasons: the grade cues are proposed card rows, and the E50 rulebook line says grading is a judgment

questions.q: Which base is this?
questions.story: A leader falls 21% in a rounded U over 14 weeks. It climbs back within 4% of the high. Then it drifts 6% lower for eight days.
choices: A cup with a handle at the rim
A flat base ending in a dip
A VCP of shrinking dips
A high tight flag

wrong.A flat base ending in a dip: Too deep and too rounded for a box.
wrong.A VCP of shrinking dips: One rounded decline and one handle, not a series of shrinking pullbacks.
wrong.A high tight flag: A high tight flag pauses 5 to 30 sessions with no rounded decline. This one rounded down over 14 weeks.

questions.answer: A cup with a handle at the rim
questions.why: A cup with a handle. A flat base falls 15% or less and stays boxy. This leader rounded down 21% over 14 weeks, climbed back within 4% of the high, then dipped into one handle. A VCP shows two or more separate pullbacks, and a high tight flag has no rounded decline.
questions.lesson_line: Measure the depth and the shape. A deep rounded rest with a dip at the rim is a cup.
questions.simple: A flat base falls 15% or less. This one fell 21% in a rounded U and then made one handle.

deeper.trap: Two numbers sort most look-alikes. Depth: a flat base falls 15% or less, and a cup falls deeper. Pullbacks: a cup is one rounded decline and one handle, and a VCP is two or more that shrink. Check both before you name the base.

reasons: touches the held cup-depth band (D-052); 21% sits inside every option so no key depends on it

questions.q: Which one is the cup?
questions.story: Base A falls in one smooth curve, climbs back to the rim, then dips once. Base B: three pullbacks of 18%, 9% and 4%.
choices: Base A; one rounded decline
Base B; its first drop is 18%
Both; each ends in a small dip
Neither; both are plain VCPs

wrong.Base B; its first drop is 18%: Three pullbacks, each smaller than the last, is a VCP.
wrong.Both; each ends in a small dip: Only one has a single rounded decline and a handle.
wrong.Neither; both are plain VCPs: Base A is one rounded decline, a climb back to the rim and one small dip. That is a cup, not a VCP.

questions.why: Base A. A cup is one rounded decline whose right side climbs back near the old high, then one handle. Base B has three separate pullbacks of 18%, 9% and 4%, each smaller than the last. That is a VCP, not a cup.
questions.lesson_line: Count the pullbacks. One rounded decline and a handle is a cup; shrinking swings are a VCP.
questions.simple: A cup is one rounded decline and one handle, while Base B shows three shrinking pullbacks, which is a VCP.

deeper.trap: A cup's handle is also a small dip after a big one, so a cup can look like two shrinking pullbacks. The tell is the first one. A cup has one rounded decline whose right side climbs back near the old high. A VCP has separate swings, each smaller than the last.

reasons: card text for the cup and the VCP agree word for word

questions.q: What is it?
questions.story: The stock rose 120% in seven weeks. Then it paused sixteen sessions, 10% deep, just under the high.
choices: A cup with a handle at the rim
A high tight flag after a run
A flat base with a flat ceiling
A VCP of shrinking pullbacks

wrong.A cup with a handle at the rim: A cup takes at least 7 weeks to round out and handle. This stock paused only sixteen sessions, far too few.
wrong.A flat base with a flat ceiling: A flat base needs at least five weeks. This paused sixteen sessions, well short of that, after a huge run.
wrong.A VCP of shrinking pullbacks: A VCP shows two or more separate pullbacks, each smaller than the last. This shows one pause.

questions.answer: A high tight flag after a run
questions.why: A high tight flag. The stock rose 120% in 7 weeks, then paused sixteen sessions. A high tight flag pauses 5 to 30 sessions with no rounded decline. A cup follows a 30% run and takes at least 7 weeks to round out and handle, and this pause is far shorter.
questions.lesson_line: A big run and a short pause is a flag. A long rounded rest is a cup.
questions.simple: A big run, then a short pause of sixteen sessions, is a high tight flag. A cup needs at least 7 weeks.

deeper.trap: A cup follows a run of at least 30%, and this run is far bigger. Do not stop at the run. A cup also needs at least 7 weeks to round out and handle. A sixteen-session pause has no time to build one. Ask whether it rounded, or only paused.

reasons: the high tight flag pole and flag length are pending owner decisions; the story uses a 120% pole and a sixteen-session pause, inside every held option
two card rows (the cup and the high tight flag) separate the cases

questions.q: Was that loss a mistake?
questions.story: A 16-week, 19% cup after a 76% run, an 8-day handle. You followed every rule: bought 260.96, stop 257.75. It closed mid-range and faded four days to your stop.
choices: No; the stop simply did its job
Yes; the stop needed room
Yes; sell mid-range closes
No; buy back to recover it

wrong.Yes; the stop needed room: The stop only moves up. More room is a bigger loss, not a fix.
wrong.Yes; sell mid-range closes: The stop is the exit. A weak close is a first warning sign, not a sell order.
wrong.No; buy back to recover it: After a stop-out, buy again only if the setup triggers again, as a new trade with its own stop and every rule.

questions.answer: No; the stop simply did its job
questions.why: No. The stop is the exit, and the loss was the plan. The breakout closed mid-range and faded four days to the stop. A weak close is the first sign the trade is not working, not an exit by itself. Buy again only on a new trigger.
questions.lesson_line: A loss at the stop is the system working. Judge the decision, not the outcome.
questions.simple: A loss at the stop is the plan working, not a mistake, and a weak close is only a warning.

deeper.trap: A stop-out does not prove the setup was bad, and a winner does not prove it was good. Judge the decision. Was it a real trigger, an honest stop, and a size that fits the grade? After a stop-out, buy again only if the setup triggers again, as a new trade with its own stop.

reasons: story built from the unreviewed dossier example d20 and d21 (D-007)
the base grade is left out of the key and the explanation, since the story does not give it

questions.q: What does our rule allow now?
questions.story: A 10-week, 18% cup with a 5-day handle breaks out on 4.9x volume. You bought 53.11, stop 52.49. On day two it reaches 2.37R.
choices: Widen the stop to give it room
Move the stop to breakeven
Sell everything at 2.37R now
Add shares while it is strong

wrong.Widen the stop to give it room: Never wider. A tight stop is answered with breakeven.
wrong.Sell everything at 2.37R now: The first trim is a third at 3R, not everything at 2.37R.
wrong.Add shares while it is strong: Moving the stop to breakeven protects the trade. It does not call for more shares.

questions.why: Move the stop to breakeven. Our rule puts that move between 2R and 5R, ideally, and 2.37R is inside it. It is a choice, not a must. The stop only moves up, never wider. A tight stop is cheap but fragile, and the answer is breakeven, not a wider stop. In BX one dip took the 1.2% stop after 2.37R, and a breakeven stop would have saved the loss.
questions.lesson_line: A tight stop is cheap but fragile. From 2R, breakeven protects it; a wider stop never does.
questions.simple: Our rule lets the stop move to breakeven once the trade is up 2R to 5R. It never lets the stop get wider.

deeper.trap: A tight stop gets hit by normal noise, and the urge is to widen it. The answer runs the other way. The stop may move up to breakeven from 2R, and it never moves wider. In BX the trade reached 2.37R on its second session. Then one dip took out the 1.2% stop, and the stock went on without us.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B19, breakeven between 2R and 5R, 'ideally')
story built from the unreviewed dossier example d22 and d23 (D-007)

questions.q: Next morning it trades under your stop. What do you do?
questions.story: A 30-week, 23% cup; the 8-day handle rests on the 50-day. You bought 273.63, stop 266.70. The day closed 270.71, low in its range.
choices: Out at the stop, as planned
Hold; the cup is still valid
Lower the stop under the handle

wrong.Hold; the cup is still valid: The stop is the exit. The cup's shape does not move it.
wrong.Lower the stop under the handle: The stop only moves up, never down.

questions.answer: Out at the stop, as planned
questions.why: Out at the stop, as planned. A cup over 6 months old with the handle resting on the 50-day is a late, tired base. If it sets up again, that is a new trade.
questions.lesson_line: Out at the stop. A new trigger later is a new trade with its own stop.

questions.q: Did you break a rule?
questions.story: The pivot is 72.58. It gaps open and you fill at 74.57. It never trades above your fill, and the next day takes the 73.36 stop.
choices: Yes; never buy at a gap open
No; the fill was inside 4%
Yes; the stop was set too tight
No; anything under 10% is fine

wrong.Yes; never buy at a gap open: No rule bans a gap fill inside 4% of the pivot.
wrong.Yes; the stop was set too tight: A tight stop is not a rule break. The stop sits a few cents under the day's low, and it only moves up.
wrong.No; anything under 10% is fine: The chase line is 4% above the buy point. The 10% line belongs to the 10-day average, a different test.

questions.why: No. A fill 2.7% over the pivot is inside the 4% chase line, and the stop was the exit. Gap-open fills are not banned. A gap it cannot build on is the first sign the answer is no. That is a warning, not a broken rule.
questions.lesson_line: A fill inside 4% is allowed. A gap that cannot build is the warning.
questions.simple: No rule was broken, since the fill was inside the 4% chase limit and the stop did its job.

deeper.trap: SCHW gapped over the 72.58 pivot at the open and filled 2.7% above it. It closed near its high, then fell through the stop the next day without ever trading above the fill. The fill was inside the 4% line and the stop was honored, so the loss was the plan.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C28 no-chase line)
story built from the unreviewed dossier example d26 and d27 (D-007)

questions.q: IBD's 7% to 8% loss limit is the stop we use on a cup breakout.
questions.why: False. IBD's 7% to 8% is its general loss limit, a reference and not ours. Our stop sits a few cents under the buy day's or prior day's low, usually within about 3% of the buy. It is never wider than a few cents under the handle low.
questions.lesson_line: Our loss is the day's range, not a fixed percent of the price.
questions.simple: False. Our stop sits a few cents under the day's low, usually within about 3% of the buy, not 7% to 8%.

deeper.trap: A flat percent loss limit is a different system. Ours starts from the chart. Stop first, a few cents under the day's low, then the size comes from the stop. If the honest stop does not fit the risk, skip the trade. Never move the stop closer to make it fit.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A3 and A13, the stop and its usual width)

questions.q: What happens to the last third?
questions.story: A steady mover: you bought 89.22 with the stop at 86.95. A third came off at 3R and a third at 5R. Weeks later it rolls over and closes under the 21-day.
choices: Held until a close under the pivot
Sold it, as the trail line broke
