Held; the stop is at breakeven
Bought more on the dip back down

wrong.Held; the stop is at breakeven: Breakeven guards the trade. The trail sells the last third.
wrong.Held until a close under the pivot: The trail is the rising average, not the pivot.
wrong.Bought more on the dip back down: The plan only sells from here. After 5R the last third trails the average.

questions.answer: Sold it, as the trail line broke
questions.why: Sold on that close. After the thirds at 3R and 5R, the last third trails a rising average. That is the 10-day for fast movers and the 21-day for steadier ones. We sell on a close below it. AX reached 5R, then rolled over below the pivot, the case for the 21-day trail.
questions.lesson_line: Two thirds banked, one on the trail. The close under the line is the exit.
questions.simple: The last third trails the 21-day average, so a close under it is the signal to sell what is left.

deeper.example: AX was bought at 89.22 with a stop at 86.95. It reached 5R in about 7 weeks, then rolled over below the pivot. That is the example for trailing the last third under the 21-day. A faster mover would trail the 10-day instead. The trim levels are adjustable defaults.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E51 and E52)
story built from the unreviewed dossier example d06 and d07 (D-007)

questions.q: Where are the stop and the first trim?
questions.story: A quiet 7-day handle. Price clears the handle high and you fill at 64.30. The lower of that day's and the prior day's low is 63.78.
choices: Just under 63.78; a third at 3R
On 63.78; a third at 2R
Handle-low stop; out at 5R
7% under fill; half at 3R

wrong.On 63.78; a third at 2R: The stop sits a few cents under the low, not on it, and the first trim is 3R.
wrong.Handle-low stop; out at 5R: The handle low is the outer limit, not the stop. The first trim is a third at 3R.
wrong.7% under fill; half at 3R: IBD's 7% to 8% is a reference, not ours. Our stop sits a few cents under the day's low, and the first trim is a third.

questions.why: The stop goes just under 63.78, the lower of that day's and the prior day's low, by a few cents. The first trim is a third at 3R. The handle low is only the outer limit for the stop, never the stop itself.
questions.lesson_line: Entry, stop, trim, trail. Write it before the open.
questions.simple: The stop goes a few cents under the lower low, and the first trim is a third at 3R.

deeper.example: The stop is set first, and the trim levels follow from it. If a stock opens above a trim level, take that trim at the open.

reasons: the stop is computed from the story (90.72 less a few cents)
rests on the owner's rulebook (F62 and B19)
story built from the unreviewed dossier example d01 (D-007)

questions.q: Hidden ticker, the day before the breakout. Judge the handle. Take it or pass.
choices: Take it; a high, quiet handle
Pass; the handle sits too low
Pass; the handle wedges up
Take it; heavy volume shows demand

wrong.Pass; the handle sits too low: It sits above the cup's midpoint.
wrong.Take it; heavy volume shows demand: A handle should be quiet, and rising volume through it ends the setup. This one ran at 0.74x the cup's volume.

questions.answer: Take it; a high, quiet handle
questions.why: Take it. The handle sits high in the base, above the cup's midpoint, and its lows do not rise. Volume is light. FFIV's handle ran 7 days, 4.2% deep, at 0.74x the cup's volume. The next session it cleared the handle high on 2.71x volume. A good picture is not a promise, so the stop still decides.
questions.lesson_line: Check the handle's place in the base before anything else. High and quiet is the picture.
questions.simple: The handle sits high in the base, its lows do not rise, and volume is light. That is the picture we want.

deeper.trap: Judge the setup the day before, not the breakout day. By then the handle already showed what mattered: high in the base, above the cup's midpoint, lows not rising, with light volume. FFIV's handle ran at 0.74x the cup's volume. Rising volume through a handle ends the setup.

reasons: chart item built from the unreviewed dossier example d01 and d02 (D-007)
fixed before (the question once gave away its own answer)

questions.q: Hidden ticker, the day before it trades through the handle high. Judge the handle. Take it or pass.
choices: Take it; the cup is 20% deep
Pass; the handle's lows rise
Take it; it is near the highs
Pass; the cup is too short

wrong.Take it; the cup is 20% deep: The cup is fine. The handle wedges up.
wrong.Take it; it is near the highs: Near the highs is the place. The wedge is the problem.
wrong.Pass; the cup is too short: A cup spans at least 7 weeks, and 13 weeks is plenty. The handle is the problem.

questions.why: Pass. Six days of rising lows into the pivot is a wedging handle with no shakeout, and rising lows are not a handle. IBD: a wedging handle with no shakeouts is a sign to steer clear. A sound 13-week, 20% cup cannot rescue it. The scan stopped this one at a best of 0.0R.
questions.lesson_line: The cup can be fine and the handle still wrong. Rising lows, I pass.
questions.simple: Rising lows into the pivot make a wedging handle, and a wedging handle with no shakeout tends to fail.

deeper.counter: The cup can be textbook and the handle still wrong. AAPL had a 13-week, 20% cup, then six days of rising lows into the pivot with no shakeout. A handle should drift sideways to down. IBD: handles that drift lower foreshadow assertive action, and overeager ones that wedge upward tend to fail.

reasons: chart item built from the unreviewed dossier example d30 (D-007)
fixed before (the 0.0R wording was reworded)

questions.q: What do you do with the breakout?
questions.story: Your best cup sits a few cents under the pivot, above its 200-day. Overnight the market reading turns Red.
choices: Buy it; A+ cups trade anywhere
No new long; stay mostly in cash
Buy half size, tight stop
Skip the cup; short the stock

wrong.Buy it; A+ cups trade anywhere: Red is mostly cash. The setup is off.
wrong.Buy half size, tight stop: Half size is still a new long in a Red market.
wrong.Skip the cup; short the stock: Our Red shorts are below the 200-day, and this cup sits above it. Red means mostly cash.

questions.answer: No new long; stay mostly in cash
questions.why: No new long. A Red reading before the buy ends the setup. In a Red market we hold mostly cash, plus shorts below the 200-day. Even the best cup waits. The reading is a guide, and Red is its most defensive setting.
questions.lesson_line: A Red reading ends the cup, however good it looks. Sit on your hands.
questions.simple: Red means mostly cash, so even the best cup is off the list and we buy nothing new.

deeper.trap: The trap is the A+ exemption. In Orange only A+ setups trade, so a great cup feels like an exception in Red. It is not. Green is full risk, Yellow smaller and fewer, Orange only A+, and Red mostly cash and shorts.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (D46 and F65, the market reading as a guide)

questions.q: How many do you buy on day one?
questions.story: A correction just ended and the reading turned Green. Six leaders in one group show cups at their pivots.
choices: Most of them; Green is full risk
A few; add more as they work
None; wait a month to be sure
Six; each at half the usual size

wrong.Most of them; Green is full risk: Green allows full risk, but after a correction you start with a few, not most of them.
wrong.None; wait a month to be sure: This is the moment the best cups come. Start small, not never.
wrong.Six; each at half the usual size: The rule is about how many positions, not how big. Half size on all six is still six positions on day one.

questions.answer: A few; add more as they work
questions.why: A few, adding more only as the first ones work. After a market correction, when the reading turns Green again, we start with a few positions. We add more only as the first ones work. Zanger: the best cups come at the beginning of a market move after a good correction. The setups are good, and the pacing is the discipline.
questions.lesson_line: Green after a correction: a few positions first. Let the winners earn the next ones.
questions.simple: After a correction, start with a few positions and add more only as the first ones work. Green still allows full risk.

deeper.trap: Green allows full risk per grade, and it still does not mean six at once. We start with a few positions and add more only as the first ones work. Zanger finds the best cups at the start of a market move, so the setups are good. The pacing is the discipline.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (F68, a few positions first after a correction)

questions.q: Are you allowed to hold through the report?
questions.story: Our rule: hold through a report only if the trade is up 5R. You bought at 50.00 and the stop is 48.00. It closes today at 61.20 and reports tomorrow after the close.
choices: Yes; it is above the hold line
Yes, and add more before the report
No; sell it before the report
No; it needs a far bigger gain

wrong.Yes, and add more before the report: Holding is allowed at 5R, but there are no new buys in the 3 days before a report.
wrong.No; sell it before the report: The rule allows a hold when the trade is up 5R, and this one is.
wrong.No; it needs a far bigger gain: The line is 5R, and this trade is past it.

questions.answer: Yes; it is above the hold line
questions.why: Yes, you may hold. The rule lets a trade ride through a report only if it is up 5R. The gain here is more than five times the risk per share, so it qualifies. The same rule bars new buys in the 3 days before a report, so you hold what you have and do not add.
questions.lesson_line: Up 5R or more, you may hold through a report. Below it, you do not.
questions.simple: Yes, because the gain here is over five times the risk, and our rule needs a trade up 5R to hold through a report.

deeper.trap: The 5R line is about a trade already open. It does not let you add. Earnings are tomorrow, so we are inside the 3 days before a report and no new buys are allowed, even with this gain. Hold what you have; do not add to it.

reasons: cites only one fact
rests on the owner's rulebook B22 (hold only if up 5R), which the story states because no earlier item teaches it

questions.q: How do we take profits on a cup winner?
choices: At the cup's measured-move target
Most of it at a 20% to 25% gain
In R: thirds at 3R and 5R, trail
Sell it all at the old high

wrong.At the cup's measured-move target: Treating the target as a sure thing is a named mistake.
wrong.Most of it at a 20% to 25% gain: That is IBD's general rule, not ours. Our trims are set in R.
wrong.Sell it all at the old high: The old high sits near the pivot. That is where the trade starts, not where it ends.

questions.answer: In R: thirds at 3R and 5R, trail
questions.why: In R: a third at 3R, a third at 5R, then trail the last third. The hard rule is a third at 3R, and the levels are adjustable. IBD takes most profits at 20% to 25%, a fixed percent that is not ours. Bulkowski's measured-move target is no sure thing: only 61% reach it.
questions.lesson_line: Sell partials into strength, in R. Targets are guesses; trims are rules.
questions.simple: We take profits in R, a third at 3R and a third at 5R, then trail the last third.

deeper.counter: IBD says take most profits at 20% to 25%. Bulkowski's measured-move target is a guess, and only 61% of cups reach it. Our trims scale with the risk taken, and R is set by the stop. A third comes off at 3R and another at 5R. The last third trails the 10-day or the 21-day.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B19 and E51)
the 20% to 25% and 61% figures are web numbers that can change

questions.q: A handle that has run 12 sessions with no breakout is stale on our card.
questions.why: False. On our card a handle goes stale only after it runs past about 6 weeks, 30 sessions, with no breakout. At 12 sessions this one is still young. A dip shorter than five days is not a handle at all.
questions.lesson_line: A handle is a short pause. Past about 30 sessions with no breakout, it is a stall.
questions.simple: A handle at 12 sessions is not stale. Stale means past about 30 sessions with no breakout.

deeper.trap: Two different checks sit close together. Under 5 sessions the dip is not yet a handle, so there is nothing to call stale. Past about 30 sessions with no breakout the base is stale and the card takes it off. Young and old both mean no buy, but for different reasons.

reasons: the 30-session limit is a card proposal, a number that may be tuned
one card fact carries the key

questions.q: Take it?
questions.story: In a rising market, a leader's cup fell 42% in a rounded U. Then a tidy 8-day handle formed near the high.
choices: Take it; 8-day handle is tidy
Pass; the cup is too deep to count
Take it; IBD allows cups to 50%
Pass; an 8-day handle is short

wrong.Take it; 8-day handle is tidy: The handle passes. The cup is far too deep.
wrong.Take it; IBD allows cups to 50%: Only in a bear market. Here the market is rising.
wrong.Pass; an 8-day handle is short: Eight sessions clears the handle minimum of 5. The cup depth is what fails.

questions.answer: Pass; the cup is too deep to count
questions.why: Pass. On our card, a cup deeper than 35% outside a bear market ends the setup. This one fell 42% in a rising market. IBD says cups can run as deep as 50% in bear markets. Zanger puts cups at maybe 20% to 35% off the old high. A tidy handle does not fix a cup that fell too far.
questions.lesson_line: A tidy handle does not fix a cup that fell too far.
questions.simple: The cup fell 42%, deeper than 35%, and that is too deep outside a bear market. A tidy handle cannot fix it.

deeper.trap: Two traps. First, quoting IBD's 50% without its condition: that depth is for cups formed in a bear market. Second, letting a tidy handle rescue a deep cup. Check the market first, then the depth, and only then the handle.

reasons: rests on the held cup-depth decision D-052
a depth threshold that is a card proposal and can change

questions.q: Which one is never allowed?
questions.story: The breakout fills at 48.60. The buy day's low sits at 46.40, about 4.5% under your fill.
choices: Skip the trade; the stop is wide
Pull the stop in to 3% to fit
Wait for a tighter spot
Put the stop under the 46.40 low

wrong.Skip the trade; the stop is wide: Skipping is always allowed when the honest stop does not fit.
wrong.Wait for a tighter spot: Waiting is always allowed. No rule makes you buy this breakout. Pulling the stop in is not allowed.
wrong.Put the stop under the 46.40 low: Allowed, and it is the default: stop first, a few cents under the day's low. About 3% is only where the stop usually sits.

questions.answer: Pull the stop in to 3% to fit
questions.why: Pulling the stop in to 3% to fit is never allowed. Stop first, a few cents under the day's low. The size comes from the stop. If the honest stop does not fit the risk, skip the trade. Never move the stop closer to make it fit.
questions.lesson_line: You never pick a size and back-fit a stop inside the noise.
questions.simple: Moving the stop closer just to make the size fit is never allowed. The stop comes first and the size follows from it.

deeper.trap: Do not treat 3% as a rule that sets the stop. The rulebook says the stop usually sits within about 3% of the buy, because that is where the day's low usually falls. Start from the honest stop, never from a percent you want.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook A3 and A4
wrong note fixed before in the cold check

questions.q: What does our rule say to do?
questions.story: Weeks after the breakout, your cup winner posts three up days in a row. The last two gap up overnight. Range widens on two of the three days, and volume rises on two days.
choices: Sell a big part into the run
Add; it is breaking out again
Do nothing; let the trail decide
Sell a small slice, hold the rest

wrong.Add; it is breaking out again: Our rule for a climax run is to sell a big part, not add. A burst is where we sell into strength.
wrong.Do nothing; let the trail decide: The trail handles the slow exit. For a climax run our rule is to sell a big part into it.
wrong.Sell a small slice, hold the rest: Our rule says a big part, not a small slice. How big is a judgment call.

questions.answer: Sell a big part into the run
questions.why: Sell a big part into the run. For a climax run on your own long, our rule is to sell a big part. How much is a judgment call. That is Bracco's parabolic burst, a 3 to 5 day final leg. It shows as up days, gap ups, range expansion and rising volume.
questions.lesson_line: A climax run is a gift. Sell a big part into it.
questions.simple: When a winner runs up in a burst of gap ups and rising volume, we sell a big part into it.

deeper.trap: Not every strong run is a climax. The burst is a short final leg of 3 to 5 days with several boxes checked: up days, overnight gap ups, range expansion and rising volume. One big day is not it. Even then the share to sell is a judgment call, with no formula.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook C34, a judgment call
how big a 'big part' is stays the owner's judgment

questions.q: Tap the number that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: We buy leaders: an RS rating of ___ or more, in one of the strongest groups.
questions.why: 80. Our rulebook buys leaders: an RS rating of 80 or more, in one of the strongest groups. The exceptions are parabolic and mean-reversion trades.
questions.lesson_line: Buy leaders: an RS rating of 80 or more, in a strong group.
questions.simple: We buy leaders, so the stock needs an RS rating of 80 or more and a place in one of the strongest groups.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook C31
the cutoff of 80 is a rule that could be retuned

questions.q: Which cup do you take?
questions.story: Two clean cups trigger the same morning. One stock has an RS rating of 92 in a top group. The other has a rating of 55 in a weak group.
choices: The 92 cup in the strong group
The 55 cup, since it has more room
Both, each at half the usual size
Neither; skip both cups today

wrong.The 55 cup, since it has more room: A weak rating in a weak group is a laggard. We buy leaders, 80 or more.
wrong.Both, each at half the usual size: Half size does not make a laggard a leader. The 55 cup fails the leader test.
wrong.Neither; skip both cups today: The 92 cup is a leader in a strong group, so it passes the leader test. Nothing in the story fails it.

questions.answer: The 92 cup in the strong group
questions.why: The 92 cup. We buy leaders: an RS rating of 80 or more, in one of the strongest groups. The 55 stock in a weak group fails that test, even with a clean chart.
questions.lesson_line: A clean chart on a laggard is still a laggard. Buy the leader.
questions.simple: Take the 92 cup. We buy leaders with an RS rating of 80 or more, and 55 in a weak group is a laggard.

deeper.trap: The trap is letting a clean chart override the leader test. Both cups look clean, so shape cannot separate them. The leader test can. The only exceptions in the rulebook are parabolic and mean-reversion trades, and neither is a cup.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook C31

questions.q: What does our rule say?
questions.story: A stock grows sales and earnings every quarter. Its cup is a sharp V, with a 5-day dip at the rim. Price trades through the handle high.
choices: Pass; the chart comes first
Pass; the handle is too short
Buy; the growth outweighs the shape
Buy half size and trim fast

wrong.Buy; the growth outweighs the shape: We prefer growth, but the chart comes first. V-shaped patterns are less reliable.
wrong.Buy half size and trim fast: Small size does not fix a failed shape. The chart comes first.
wrong.Pass; the handle is too short: A 5-day dip meets the 5-session handle minimum. The V cup is what fails.

questions.why: Pass; the chart comes first. We prefer growing sales and earnings, but the chart decides first. On our card a cup that is a V ends the setup before the buy, and IBD says V-shaped patterns are less reliable. Strong growth does not rescue the shape.
questions.lesson_line: Growth is a plus. The chart decides first.
questions.simple: Pass. We like growth, but the chart comes first, and a sharp V cup fails the chart.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook D40

questions.q: A clean cup breakout is fine to buy even when price sits under its 200-day average.
questions.why: False. Our rule is no longs below the 200-day simple moving average, unless it is a parabolic long. A cup with a handle is not a parabolic long, so a clean shape does not change it. The card also tests that price is above the 200-day at the buy.
questions.lesson_line: No long under the 200-day. A tidy cup does not change that.
questions.simple: False. We do not buy a long under its 200-day average, and a clean cup is not a parabolic long.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook B26

questions.q: The cup is clean and price trades through the 31.40 pivot. The 200-day average is 33.10. Which rule decides this?
choices: No longs under the 200-day average
No chasing more than 4% over the pivot
No new buys within 3 days of earnings
Skip longs over 10% above the 10-day

wrong.No chasing more than 4% over the pivot: The buy is at the pivot, so there is no chase. The 200-day is the issue.
wrong.No new buys within 3 days of earnings: Nothing here mentions a report. The 200-day average decides this one.
wrong.Skip longs over 10% above the 10-day: The story gives no 10-day average and price is at the pivot. The 200-day average decides this one.

questions.why: No longs under the 200-day average. Price trades through the 31.40 pivot, but the 200-day is 33.10, so price is under it. Our rule bans longs below the 200-day unless it is a parabolic long, and a cup is not one. The pivot test never gets a vote.
questions.lesson_line: Check the 200-day before the pivot. Under it, no long.
questions.simple: Price is under its 200-day average, and we do not buy longs under that line.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook B26

questions.q: A cup stock averages 600,000 shares a day at $28. How many millions of dollars does it trade a day?
questions.why: 16.8 million dollars a day. Dollars traded is price times shares: $28 times 600,000. Our floor is a price of $10 or more and at least $20 million traded a day. This stock clears the price but not the dollar floor, so we skip it, however clean the cup.
questions.lesson_line: Price times shares is dollars traded. We need $20 million a day.
questions.simple: It trades 16.8 million dollars a day, which is under the 20 million we need, so we skip it.

reasons: a computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook (B23)

questions.q: A $7 stock that trades $40 million a day passes our liquidity floor.
questions.why: False. We trade only stocks at $10 or more that trade at least $20 million a day. Both tests must pass. At $7 the stock fails the price test, even though $40 million a day clears the dollar-volume test.
questions.lesson_line: Both tests count: $10 a share and $20 million a day.
questions.simple: False. Both tests must pass, and a $7 stock fails the $10 price minimum even with big dollar volume.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook B23

questions.q: We never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume. A stock averages 250,000 shares a day. What is the most we may own?
questions.why: 2,500 shares. We never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume. One percent of 250,000 is 2,500. It is a ceiling on what we own, and it applies to every stock.
questions.lesson_line: Cap every position at 1% of average daily volume.
questions.simple: We may own at most 1% of average daily volume, and 1% of 250,000 shares is 2,500.

reasons: a computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook (D42)

questions.q: What is the most you may buy?
questions.story: The risk math and the position cap allow 5,000 shares of a cup breakout. The stock averages 220,000 shares a day. You hold none today.
choices: 2,200 shares
5,000 shares
3,600 shares
1,100 shares

wrong.5,000 shares: The risk math sets a size, but this is over 1% of average daily volume. The volume cap wins.
wrong.3,600 shares: Averaging the two limits is not a rule. It is still over 1% of average daily volume.
wrong.1,100 shares: That is half the cap. The question asks for the most you may buy, and that is the cap.

questions.why: 2,200 shares. The risk math allows 5,000, but we never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume. One percent of 220,000 is 2,200, the lower limit, so the volume cap sets the most you may buy.
questions.lesson_line: Never own more than 1% of average daily volume, whatever the risk math allows.
questions.simple: Buy at most 2,200 shares, because 1% of 220,000 is 2,200 and that is below the 5,000 the risk math allows.

deeper.trap: The cap counts what you own, not one order. Buying the cap now and the same again later leaves double the cap held. Averaging the two limits gives 3,600, still over the cap.

reasons: a computed key (220,000 / 100)
rests on the owner's rulebook D42; the story says the risk math and the position cap allow 5,000, so the volume cap is the only extra limit

questions.q: On our card, the down weeks on a cup's left side roughly match the up weeks on its right side.
questions.why: True. IBD says the number of down weeks on the left side should roughly match the number of up weeks on the right side. Our card uses the same cue. The match is rough, not exact. A lopsided cup grades down.
questions.lesson_line: A good cup is symmetric: weeks down on the left, weeks up on the right.
questions.simple: True. A good cup is balanced, with the weeks down on the left roughly equal to the weeks up on the right.

reasons: the symmetry cue is a card cue with IBD as the main source

questions.q: A cup has 8 down weeks on its left side and 2 up weeks on its right. What does the symmetry cue say?
choices: Lopsided, so it grades lower
Lopsided, but it grades the same
Strong, a fast climb back is best
Fine, if the handle is quiet

wrong.Fine, if the handle is quiet: A quiet handle is a separate cue. It does not fix a lopsided cup.
wrong.Lopsided, but it grades the same: Lopsided is right, but the card does not grade it the same. A lopsided cup grades down.
wrong.Strong, a fast climb back is best: A fast climb back is not the goal. IBD wants the up weeks on the right to roughly match the down weeks on the left.

questions.why: Lopsided, so it grades lower. IBD wants the down weeks on the left to roughly match the up weeks on the right. 8 against 2 is far apart. Our card grades a lopsided cup down.
questions.lesson_line: Count the weeks down and the weeks up. They should roughly match.
questions.simple: A cup with 8 down weeks and only 2 up weeks is lopsided, so it grades lower.

reasons: the symmetry cue is a card cue with IBD as the main source

questions.q: A typical handle forms over about one to four weeks.
questions.why: True. AAII says a handle typically forms over about one to four weeks. StockCharts says it is ideally completed within one to four weeks, though a handle can last longer. Our card says usually 1 to 4 weeks, and grades one over about 22 sessions down.
questions.lesson_line: A typical handle runs one to four weeks.
questions.simple: True. A typical handle takes about one to four weeks, and AAII and StockCharts agree.

reasons: the 22-session grading line is a card proposal
AAII also says longer handles can signal bigger moves, so sources are not fully aligned

questions.q: What does our card do with it?
questions.story: A cup has a quiet handle. Its lows drift down and every close holds above the 50-day. It has now run 24 sessions with no breakout.
choices: Grade it down; keep it listed
Drop it; the handle is stale
Grade it up; a long handle is best
Buy now, before it gets older

wrong.Drop it; the handle is stale: Stale starts past about 30 sessions. This handle is at 24.
wrong.Grade it up; a long handle is best: Long handles grade down. A typical handle runs 1 to 4 weeks.
wrong.Buy now, before it gets older: The buy is the trade through the handle high. No trade, no buy.

questions.answer: Grade it down; keep it listed
questions.why: Grade it down; keep it on the list. The card grades a handle over about 22 sessions down, and this one is at 24. It goes stale, and comes off, only past about 30 sessions with no breakout. The falling lows and the 50-day hold are what a good handle shows, so it stays on the list.
questions.lesson_line: Handles over about 22 sessions grade down. Past about 30 they are stale.
questions.simple: A handle over about 22 sessions is graded down. It is stale only past about 30 sessions, and this one is at 24.

deeper.trap: Two different lines. About 22 sessions is where the grade drops. About 30 sessions is where the card takes the setup off. In between it is still live, only graded lower. Neither line is a buy signal: the buy is still the trade through the handle high.

reasons: the 22 and 30 session lines are card proposals
AAII's remark that longer handles can signal bigger moves differs from the card's grade-down rule

questions.q: Handle high 50.00, handle low 47.50. How deep is the handle, in percent?
questions.why: 5.0%. Depth is the fall from the handle's own high, taken as a percent of that high. Our card calls a handle of 8% or less better, and about 5% best. Zanger's 5% is measured from the old high point, which is a different yardstick.
questions.lesson_line: Handle depth is the fall from its own high. Shallower grades higher.
questions.simple: Depth is the fall from the handle's own high as a percent, and here that is 5.0%.

reasons: a computed key
the 8% and 5% grade cues are card numbers

questions.q: Which handle grades highest on our card?
questions.story: Three clean cups, each with a quiet handle that drifts down. The handles are 5%, 7% and 11% deep.
choices: The 5% deep handle
The 7% handle
The 11% handle
They grade alike

wrong.They grade alike: Depth counts on our card: 8% or less is better, and about 5% is best.
wrong.The 7% handle: Good, since 8% or less is better, but about 5% is best.
wrong.The 11% handle: 11% is past 8%, so it grades lower. A deeper handle gives back more.

questions.why: The 5% handle. Our card grades a handle of 8% or less better, and about 5% best. The 7% handle is under 8%, so it is good but not best. The 11% handle is past 8%, so it grades lower. IBD says a handle's secondary decline is usually no more than 8% to 12%. So 11% is a lower grade, not a different pattern.
questions.lesson_line: Handles of 8% or less grade better. About 5% is best.
questions.simple: The 5% handle grades highest. Our card likes 8% or less, and about 5% is best.

deeper.trap: Do not read 'grades highest' as 'the others fail'. All three handles can be valid. The card prefers 8% or less and about 5% best, and IBD's usual range for a handle's dip runs up to about 8% to 12%. The 11% handle simply earns a lower grade.

reasons: the 8% and 5% cues are card numbers that may be retuned
close to the pending handle-depth decision D-053 but not keyed on it

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: IBD says a handle should generally form ___ the 50-day or 10-week moving average.
questions.why: Above. IBD says a handle should generally form above the 50-day or 10-week moving averages. Our card is stricter: a close below the 50-day during the handle ends the setup before the buy.
questions.lesson_line: A good handle holds above the 50-day.
questions.simple: A handle should generally sit above the 50-day line, and our card wants no close under it.

reasons: the card's one-close test is stricter than IBD's 'generally', a card proposal

questions.q: What does our rule say about that plan?
questions.story: You bought a cup breakout at 54.57 with the stop at 52.94. You plan to watch the screen and sell by hand if it breaks 52.94.
choices: Enter the stop as a real order
Fine, if you stay at the screen
Fine, a stop this tight is safe
Set a price alert and sell by hand

wrong.Fine, if you stay at the screen: You cannot watch every moment, and a stop kept in your head is not a stop.
wrong.Fine, a stop this tight is safe: A tight stop does not make a mental one safe. The order goes in with the broker.
wrong.Set a price alert and sell by hand: An alert is a reminder, not an order. Every position has a real stop order.

questions.answer: Enter the stop as a real order
questions.why: Enter the stop as a real order. Our rule is that every position has a real stop order with the broker, not a stop kept in your head. Watching the screen depends on you being there at the right moment, and a price alert is only a reminder. The stop at 52.94 also only moves up.
questions.lesson_line: A stop in your head is not a stop. Put the order in.
questions.simple: Enter the stop as a real order with the broker, because a stop kept in your head is not a stop.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook D41

questions.q: Apart from the gap rule, our stop only ever moves up, never down or wider.
questions.why: True. The stop is the exit. It only moves up, never down or wider. The one exception is the gap rule. After a gap through the stop, the low of the first 30-minute bar becomes the new stop.
questions.lesson_line: The stop only moves up. The gap rule is the one exception.
questions.simple: True. The stop only moves up, and the gap rule is the one exception.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook A4 and D41

questions.q: What do you do with the first third?
questions.story: You bought at 91.29 with the stop at 90.67, so 3R is 93.15. The next morning the stock opens at 94.20.
choices: Sell that third at the open
Wait for a dip to 93.15
Sell two thirds at open
Sell it at the close

wrong.Wait for a dip to 93.15: Our rule is to take it at the open, not to bet on a pullback.
wrong.Sell it at the close: The rule says at the open.
wrong.Sell two thirds at open: The first trim is a third at 3R, not two thirds.

questions.answer: Sell that third at the open
questions.why: Sell that third at the open. The first trim is a third at 3R, and if a stock opens above a trim level we take that trim at the open. Here 3R was 93.15 and the stock opened at 94.20, above it.
questions.lesson_line: A gap over the trim level means you take the trim at the open.
questions.simple: When a stock opens above a trim level, we sell that trim at the open and do not wait.

deeper.trap: Do not treat 93.15 as a limit order sitting in the market. When a stock gaps over it, the price you can get is the open. Waiting for a fall back to 93.15 is a bet that it comes. The 5R trim, another third, comes later.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook B19 and F63

questions.q: If a stock opens above 3R, we wait for it to fall back to 3R before we trim.
questions.why: False. The rule is that if a stock opens above a trim level (3R or 5R), we take that trim at the open. Waiting for a pullback to 3R is a bet that the pullback comes, and the rule does not make that bet.
questions.lesson_line: Opens above a trim level: take that trim at the open.
questions.simple: False. When a stock opens above a trim level, we take the trim at the open and do not wait for a pullback.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook F63

questions.q: Before the buy, a quiet handle is still off the list if its midpoint sits below the cup's midpoint.
questions.why: True. Our card ends the setup before the buy if the handle's midpoint sits below the cup's midpoint. IBD wants the handle's midpoint above the cup's midpoint, and says handles that form too low present added risk of failure. Quiet volume does not make up for a handle that is too low.
questions.lesson_line: Quiet is not enough. The handle must sit above the cup's midpoint.
questions.simple: True. A handle must sit above the middle of the cup, and a handle that sits lower is too low to buy.

reasons: the card's midpoint test is a proposal with IBD behind it

questions.q: Before the buy, what do those lows make of the handle?
questions.story: A clean cup, then a 6-session handle. Its lows run 47.0, 47.2, 47.4, 47.6, 47.9 and 48.3. Volume is quiet.
choices: A wedging handle; it often fails
A tight handle; grades best
A short handle; not counted
A flat handle; it passes

wrong.A tight handle; grades best: Tight closes are a separate cue. These lows climb, so the line trends up.
wrong.A short handle; not counted: Six sessions clears the 5-session minimum. The rising lows are what fail.
wrong.A flat handle; it passes: Flat lows would pass, but these climb from 47.0 to 48.3. A line through them slopes up.

questions.answer: A wedging handle; it often fails
questions.why: A wedging handle; it often fails. A straight line through those six lows slopes up, and the card wants it flat or down. Rising lows end the setup before the buy. IBD says wedging handles have a higher failure rate, and a wedging handle with no shakeouts is a sign to steer clear. Quiet volume does not fix it.
questions.lesson_line: Fit a line through the handle's lows. It must slope flat or down.
questions.simple: The lows climb every session, which makes a wedge, and wedging handles fail more often.

deeper.trap: Quiet volume is not proof of a good handle. Volume is one test and the slope of the lows is another, and both must pass. IBD says handles that drift lower foreshadow assertive action, while rising lows with no shakeout are a wedge to steer clear of.

reasons: the slope test is a card proposal with IBD behind it

questions.q: A 4-session dip under the rim becomes a handle if the breakout comes on heavy volume.
questions.why: False. IBD says if it's shorter than five days, it's not a handle. Our card also needs a handle of at least 5 sessions, and a shorter one ends the setup before the buy. Breakout volume is a separate cue and does not change the count of a 4-session dip.
questions.lesson_line: Under five sessions is not a handle, whatever the volume.
questions.simple: False. A dip shorter than five days is not a handle, so heavy breakout volume cannot rescue it.

deeper.trap: Do not let a strong breakout argue the setup into shape. Count the sessions first: at least 5. A named mistake on the card is calling a 2 or 3-day dip a handle, and a 4-day dip is only a little longer.

reasons: IBD and the card agree on the 5-session minimum

questions.q: Tap the number that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: We skip a long that is more than ___ percent above its 10-day average.
questions.why: 10. Our rulebook skips a long that is more than 10% above its 10-day average, because it is too stretched to buy. The 4% line is a different test: how far past the buy point you may pay.
questions.lesson_line: More than 10% above the 10-day is too stretched. Skip it.
questions.simple: A long more than 10% above its 10-day average is too stretched to buy.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C29, settled)
added so the stretch rule is taught before q43 applies it

questions.q: On a gap down through our stop, we get out at once if the first 30 minutes take the loss past 2R.
questions.why: True. On a gap through the stop, the first 30 minutes of the gap-down day decide. The low of the first 30-minute bar is the new stop, with a ceiling: past 2R, get out.
questions.lesson_line: A gap through the stop has a ceiling: past 2R in the first 30 minutes, get out.
questions.simple: On a gap through the stop, the first 30 minutes decide. If they take the loss past 2R, get out.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B20, the gap rule and its 2R ceiling)
added so the gap rule and its ceiling are taught before q32 applies them

questions.story: A cup breakout triggers at 48.60. The buy day's low is 46.40, so the honest stop goes a few cents under it. At that stop your size comes out smaller than you hoped.
questions.q: You want more shares. What does our rule say?
choices: Keep the stop; let it set the size
Pull the stop in for more shares
Keep the usual size and risk more
Keep the stop; round the size up
questions.answer: Keep the stop; let it set the size

wrong.Pull the stop in for more shares: Never move the stop closer to make the size fit. The size follows the stop, not the other way round.
wrong.Keep the usual size and risk more: Shares come from account times risk percent, divided by entry minus stop. The stop sets the size; you do not stretch the risk.
wrong.Keep the stop; round the size up: The share count is rounded down, never up.

questions.simple: Never move the stop closer to make the size fit. The stop comes first and the size follows from it.
questions.why: Keep the stop and let it set the size. Stop first, a few cents under the day's low. Never move the stop closer to make it fit. If the honest stop does not fit the risk, skip the trade.
questions.lesson_line: You never pick a size and back-fit a stop. The stop comes first.

deeper.trap: The trap is pulling the stop in to get the size you wanted. Start from the honest stop, a few cents under the day's low, and take the size it gives. If that size does not fit the risk, skip the trade.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook A3 and A5
no percent is keyed, so the pending stop-width decision is not leaned on

questions.q: On our card, what is your call on this handle?
questions.story: A rounded 10-week cup falls 20%, then a handle forms in its upper half. The handle drifts down for eight sessions above the 50-day. Volume rises every session, and the handle's average tops the cup's.
choices: Pass; a loud handle ends the setup
Buy; rising volume shows demand
Buy the pivot; the lows drift down fine
Pass; eight sessions is too short
questions.answer: Pass; a loud handle ends the setup

wrong.Buy; rising volume shows demand: A handle should go quiet. On our card, volume rising through the handle ends the setup.
wrong.Buy the pivot; the lows drift down fine: The drift passes, but volume is a separate test. Rising volume ends the setup on its own.
wrong.Pass; eight sessions is too short: A handle needs at least 5 sessions, so eight clears it. The volume is what fails.

questions.why: Pass. On our card, volume that rises through the handle ends the setup before the buy. The handle should also average below the cup's volume, and this one averages above it. IBD says volume should dry up, evidence that the weak holders are just about gone. Here it climbs instead, so the drift and the 50-day do not save it.
questions.lesson_line: A handle should go quiet. Volume that climbs through it ends the setup.
questions.simple: A loud handle ends the setup on our card, so you pass even though its shape and the 50-day look fine.

reasons: the volume gate is a proposed card row, not an owner ruling
IBD gives the direction of handle volume, no number
the story fails both readings of the row: a rising trend and an average above the cup's
